## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 236 — WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance: Verifying Minimum Focus Indicator Area and Contrast [official]

WCAG 2.4.13 (AAA) requires that the focus indicator area is at least as large as a 2 CSS pixel perimeter around the unfocused component, and that the contrast ratio between focused and unfocused states is at least 3:1. Many custom components pass 2.4.7 (Focus Visible) with a faint ring but silently fail the stronger 2.4.13 area-and-contrast requirement. Automated tools do not yet detect this reliably, making scripted visual measurement the only scalable approach.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('focus indicator meets WCAG 2.4.13 minimum area and contrast', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/components/button');

  const button = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Subscribe' });

  // Measure bounding box before focusing
  const unfocused = await button.boundingBox();

  // Tab to button
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
  await expect(button).toBeFocused();

  // Capture focused state screenshot for visual comparison
  const focusedScreenshot = await button.screenshot();
  expect(focusedScreenshot).toBeTruthy();

  // Verify button has a CSS focus-visible style applied
  const outlineStyle = await button.evaluate((el) => {
    const styles = window.getComputedStyle(el, ':focus-visible');
    return {
      outlineWidth: styles.outlineWidth,
      outlineColor: styles.outlineColor,
      outlineStyle: styles.outlineStyle,
    };
  });

  // outline-width must be at least 2px to form an adequate perimeter
  const outlineWidthPx = parseFloat(outlineStyle.outlineWidth);
  expect(outlineWidthPx).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);

  // outline-style must not be 'none'
  expect(outlineStyle.outlineStyle).not.toBe('none');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Playwright can verify that `outline-width >= 2px` and `outline-style != none`, but it cannot directly compute the WCAG 2.4.13 contrast ratio between the focused outline pixel colour and the adjacent background pixel — that requires pixel-level colour sampling from a screenshot (e.g., Jimp or sharp in Node.js). Teams often enforce a design token constraint (`--focus-ring-color` must satisfy 3:1 against `--surface-color`) at the design-system level and write a one-time token audit script rather than per-test pixel sampling. [official]

---

### Pattern 237 — WCAG 3.2.6 Consistent Help: Asserting Help Mechanism Position Across Pages [official]

WCAG 3.2.6 (A, new in 2.2) requires that if a help mechanism (live chat widget, "Contact Us" link, FAQ link, support phone number) appears on multiple pages, it must appear in the same relative order to other page content on every page. This criterion exists primarily to aid users with cognitive disabilities who rely on consistent page structure to locate support. Testing requires comparing the DOM order of the help element relative to surrounding landmarks across a representative set of pages.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const pagesToCheck = ['/', '/products', '/checkout', '/account'];

test('help mechanism appears in consistent DOM order across pages (WCAG 3.2.6)', async ({ page }) => {
  const helpPositions: number[] = [];

  for (const url of pagesToCheck) {
    await page.goto(url);

    // Find the help/support link by its accessible name
    const allLinks = await page.getByRole('link').all();
    let helpIndex = -1;

    for (let i = 0; i < allLinks.length; i++) {
      const name = await allLinks[i].getAttribute('aria-label') ??
                   await allLinks[i].innerText();
      if (/help|support|contact|chat/i.test(name)) {
        helpIndex = i;
        break;
      }
    }

    expect(helpIndex).toBeGreaterThan(-1); // help link must exist on every page
    helpPositions.push(helpIndex);
  }

  // The relative position should be the same (first occurrence) across all pages
  // Allow variance of ±2 positions to account for page-specific content
  const min = Math.min(...helpPositions);
  const max = Math.max(...helpPositions);
  expect(max - min).toBeLessThanOrEqual(2);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** DOM order index is a proxy for "relative order" but is not the same as visual position. A help widget rendered via a CSS sticky footer may have a late DOM index but always appear visually at the bottom. WCAG 3.2.6 focuses on relative order in the page's content flow. The best test strategy is to assert the help mechanism is within the same landmark region (e.g., always inside `<footer>` or always inside the main content area) rather than relying on raw DOM index, which is fragile and can change with minor page restructuring. [official]

---

### Pattern 238 — WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry: Verifying Auto-Population of Previously Entered Data [official]

WCAG 3.3.7 (A, new in 2.2) requires that when a multi-step process asks users to re-enter information they already provided in the same session, the system either auto-populates the field or provides an option to select the previously entered value. The most common failure is checkout flows that require re-entering a shipping address in the billing section without a "same as shipping" option. Testing this criterion requires simulating a complete multi-step flow and asserting that fields are pre-populated or that a copy mechanism exists.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('billing address auto-populates from shipping entry (WCAG 3.3.7)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/shipping');

  // Step 1: Fill shipping address
  await page.getByLabel('Street address').fill('123 Elm Street');
  await page.getByLabel('City').fill('Springfield');
  await page.getByLabel('Post code').fill('62701');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to payment' }).click();

  // Step 2: Assert billing section either:
  //   (a) Pre-populates with the same values, OR
  //   (b) Offers a "Same as shipping address" checkbox
  await page.waitForURL('**/checkout/payment');

  const sameAsShipping = page.getByRole('checkbox', {
    name: /same as shipping/i,
  });

  const billingStreet = page.getByLabel(/billing.*street|street.*billing/i);

  const hasCopyOption = await sameAsShipping.count() > 0;
  const hasPrePopulatedField = hasCopyOption
    ? false
    : await billingStreet.inputValue().then((v) => v === '123 Elm Street');

  expect(hasCopyOption || hasPrePopulatedField).toBe(true);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** This test is inherently end-to-end and stateful — it requires a working checkout session and may conflict with parallel test runs that share backend cart state. Teams should use isolated test users or a mocked checkout API to avoid flakiness. Additionally, the WCAG exception for "security-critical re-entry" (e.g., re-entering a credit card number) means not every repeated field is a failure; tests should document which fields are intentionally exempt. [official]

---

### Pattern 239 — WCAG 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication: Detecting Cognitive-Function-Only Login Barriers [official]

WCAG 3.3.8 (AA, new in 2.2) prohibits authentication flows that require only a cognitive function test (memorising a password, solving a visual puzzle, transcribing distorted characters) without offering an alternative. Acceptable alternatives include a password manager-compatible `autocomplete` attribute, object recognition (identifying pictures of objects the user has selected), or personal content (recognising a photo the user uploaded). Testing covers: (1) that password fields have `autocomplete="current-password"`, (2) that CAPTCHA alternatives exist, (3) that paste is not blocked.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('login form meets WCAG 3.3.8 accessible authentication requirements', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');

  // 1. Password field must support autocomplete (password manager access)
  const passwordInput = page.getByLabel(/password/i);
  const autocomplete = await passwordInput.getAttribute('autocomplete');
  expect(autocomplete).toBe('current-password');

  // 2. Paste must not be blocked on password field
  await passwordInput.click();
  await page.keyboard.press('Control+v'); // attempt paste
  // If paste is blocked, the field stays empty; we detect via event listener
  const pasteBlocked = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const input = document.querySelector('input[type="password"]') as HTMLInputElement;
    let blocked = false;
    input.addEventListener('paste', (e) => { if (e.defaultPrevented) blocked = true; });
    return blocked;
  });
  expect(pasteBlocked).toBe(false);

  // 3. If a CAPTCHA is present, an alternative must exist
  const hasCaptcha = await page.locator('[class*="captcha"], [id*="captcha"]').count() > 0;
  if (hasCaptcha) {
    const hasAlternative = await page.getByRole('link', {
      name: /audio captcha|contact support|alternative/i,
    }).count() > 0;
    expect(hasAlternative).toBe(true);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Blocking the paste event is a common but incorrect security measure — clipboard content can still be captured by malware, so paste-blocking provides no genuine security while punishing users who rely on password managers. Many organisations resist removing paste-blocking because it is a policy decision rather than a technical one; in these cases, the Playwright test serves as a documented WCAG 3.3.8 failure that can be escalated through compliance channels rather than fixed immediately in the codebase. [official]

---

### Pattern 240 — axe-core `resultTypes` Optimisation: Limiting Selector Computation on Large DOM Pages [official]

For pages with more than 50,000 DOM elements (dashboard-heavy enterprise UIs, data grid views), running `axe.run()` without constraint causes axe to compute full CSS selectors for every pass and inapplicable result — not just violations — multiplying execution time by 4–8x. Setting `resultTypes: ['violations', 'incomplete']` restricts selector computation to only the result categories the test cares about, reducing scan time from 30+ seconds to under 5 seconds on very large pages while preserving all actionable output.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('large data grid page: axe scan with resultTypes optimisation', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard/data-grid?rows=5000');

  // Wait for the full grid to render
  await page.waitForSelector('[role="grid"] [role="row"]');

  const start = Date.now();

  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .options({
      // Only compute selectors for violations and items needing manual review
      resultTypes: ['violations', 'incomplete'],
    })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa'])
    .analyze();

  const duration = Date.now() - start;
  console.log(`axe scan completed in ${duration}ms`);

  // Duration guard: fail if scan takes longer than 10 seconds
  expect(duration).toBeLessThan(10_000);

  // Filter for high-impact violations only
  const criticalViolations = results.violations.filter(
    (v) => v.impact === 'critical' || v.impact === 'serious',
  );

  expect(criticalViolations).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Restricting `resultTypes` to `['violations', 'incomplete']` means the `passes` array will be empty, so teams that use `passes` for coverage reporting (e.g., "X rules passed across Y elements") will lose that metric. This is an acceptable tradeoff for performance-sensitive pages. For summary reporting, run a full scan (without `resultTypes` restriction) on a representative sample page rather than on every page in the suite. [official]

---

### Pattern 241 — ARIA Combobox Pattern: Keyboard Navigation and `aria-expanded` State Testing [official]

The ARIA combobox pattern (APG) requires a text input (`role="combobox"`) paired with a popup listbox. The input must have `aria-haspopup="listbox"`, `aria-expanded` toggling between `true`/`false`, and `aria-controls` pointing to the listbox ID. Keyboard contract: `Down Arrow` opens the popup and moves focus into the list; `Escape` closes the popup and returns focus to the input; `Enter` confirms selection and closes. Custom autocomplete components frequently skip the `aria-expanded` toggle, leaving screen readers unable to announce popup state changes.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('combobox keyboard contract and ARIA state (APG combobox pattern)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/components/autocomplete');

  const combobox = page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Country' });

  // Initial state: collapsed
  await expect(combobox).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');

  // Type to open popup
  await combobox.fill('Can');
  await expect(combobox).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');

  // Listbox must be present in the DOM
  const listboxId = await combobox.getAttribute('aria-controls');
  expect(listboxId).toBeTruthy();
  const listbox = page.locator(`#${listboxId}`);
  await expect(listbox).toBeVisible();

  // Arrow Down moves focus to first option
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowDown');
  const focusedOption = page.locator(`#${listboxId} [role="option"][aria-selected="true"],
    #${listboxId} [role="option"]:focus`).first();
  await expect(focusedOption).toBeVisible();

  // Escape closes popup and returns focus to input
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(combobox).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  await expect(combobox).toBeFocused();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The ARIA APG combobox pattern has evolved significantly between ARIA 1.1 and ARIA 1.2. In the ARIA 1.1 pattern, `aria-activedescendant` was used to track listbox focus without moving DOM focus; in the ARIA 1.2 pattern, focus moves into the listbox. Many existing component libraries still implement the deprecated 1.1 pattern. Tests should document which pattern they are asserting to avoid confusion, and axe-core may flag components as failing the 1.2 pattern even when the 1.1 pattern is intentionally used. [official]

---

### Pattern 242 — ARIA Disclosure Widget: `aria-expanded` and Heading-Level Pairing [official]

The ARIA APG Disclosure pattern describes a button that shows or hides a section of content, where `aria-expanded` communicates the current state. A common failure is using a plain `<div>` as the toggle instead of a `<button>`, or nesting a `<button>` inside a heading element (`<h2><button>...</button></h2>`). The heading-button combination is valid in HTML5 and required by the Accordion pattern (APG), but the `<button>` element must be a direct child of the heading, not a sibling element styled to look like part of the heading.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('disclosure widget: aria-expanded toggles and content visibility', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/components/disclosure');

  const triggers = await page.getByRole('button', { expanded: false }).all();
  expect(triggers.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  for (const trigger of triggers) {
    const controlsId = await trigger.getAttribute('aria-controls');
    expect(controlsId).toBeTruthy();

    const panel = page.locator(`#${controlsId}`);
    const initiallyHidden =
      (await panel.isHidden()) ||
      (await panel.getAttribute('hidden')) !== null;

    // Click trigger to expand
    await trigger.click();
    await expect(trigger).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
    await expect(panel).toBeVisible();

    // Click again to collapse
    await trigger.click();
    await expect(trigger).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The test assumes `aria-controls` points to the controlled panel, but many implementations omit `aria-controls` and instead place the panel as the next DOM sibling of the button. The ARIA APG considers `aria-controls` optional for disclosure (unlike for combobox). If `aria-controls` is absent, tests must use DOM adjacency (`locator + nextSibling`) to find the panel, which is more brittle. Teams building new components should include `aria-controls` explicitly to make both tests and AT behaviour more predictable. [official]

---

### Pattern 243 — ARIA `role="status"` vs `role="alert"`: Choosing the Right Live Region Politeness Level [official]

`role="status"` (equivalent to `aria-live="polite"`) announces messages after the current speech has finished; `role="alert"` (equivalent to `aria-live="assertive"`) interrupts speech immediately. Misusing `role="alert"` for non-critical updates (e.g., "3 items in your cart") creates a disruptive experience for screen reader users, while using `role="status"` for genuinely critical messages (e.g., "Session expired") causes announcements to be delayed or missed. The correct mapping: errors and time-sensitive warnings use `role="alert"`; progress updates, confirmations, and status messages use `role="status"`.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('shopping cart update uses polite status role (not alert)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products/widget');

  // Assert the live region uses the correct role before interaction
  const statusRegion = page.locator('[role="status"]');
  await expect(statusRegion).toHaveCount(1);

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();

  // Non-critical confirmation should be in role="status" (polite)
  await expect(statusRegion).toContainText(/added to cart|cart updated/i);
});

test('session expiry warning uses assertive alert role', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Trigger a session timeout simulation
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('session:expired'));
  });

  const alertRegion = page.locator('[role="alert"]');
  await expect(alertRegion).toBeVisible();
  await expect(alertRegion).toContainText(/session expired|please log in again/i);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `role="alert"` must be present in the DOM before content is injected into it — dynamically inserting a `<div role="alert">` with content already inside does not reliably trigger announcements in all screen reader / browser combinations (particularly NVDA + Chrome). The robust pattern is to have an empty `role="alert"` container in the initial page HTML and then inject content into it dynamically. This means tests that check `role="alert"` visibility may need to wait for content injection separately from element visibility. [official]

---

### Pattern 244 — WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements: Verifying Single-Pointer Alternatives [official]

WCAG 2.5.7 (A, new in 2.2) requires that any action achieved through dragging can also be accomplished with a single pointer (click/tap) without requiring drag. Common failures include: sortable lists where reordering is only available via drag-and-drop; range sliders that can only be adjusted by dragging the thumb; map interfaces where panning requires drag. Testing verifies that an alternative activation mechanism exists — typically a context menu, up/down button pair, or keyboard input.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('sortable list provides non-drag reordering alternative (WCAG 2.5.7)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings/column-order');

  const listItems = await page.getByRole('listitem').all();
  expect(listItems.length).toBeGreaterThan(1);

  // Each draggable item must have a single-pointer alternative
  for (const item of listItems) {
    // Look for move-up / move-down buttons within each item
    const moveUpBtn = item.getByRole('button', { name: /move up|up/i });
    const moveDownBtn = item.getByRole('button', { name: /move down|down/i });

    const hasSinglePointerAlternative =
      (await moveUpBtn.count() > 0) || (await moveDownBtn.count() > 0);

    expect(hasSinglePointerAlternative).toBe(true);
  }

  // Verify the alternative actually works: move first item down
  const firstItem = listItems[0];
  const initialText = await firstItem.innerText();
  const moveDownBtn = firstItem.getByRole('button', { name: /move down/i });
  await moveDownBtn.click();

  // After move, the second position should now contain the originally-first item
  const updatedItems = await page.getByRole('listitem').all();
  const secondItemText = await updatedItems[1].innerText();
  expect(secondItemText).toContain(initialText.trim());
});
```

**Tradeoff.** This test is tightly coupled to the specific button labels used for the reordering alternative. Internationalised applications will use localised button labels, requiring either data attributes (e.g., `data-testid="move-up"`) or ARIA labels that remain stable across locales. Teams should standardise on `aria-label` values for move-up/move-down controls using a single canonical English string even in localised apps, driven from translation keys, to keep this test maintainable. [official]

---

### Pattern 245 — axe-core Custom Rule Registration: Enforcing Team-Specific Accessibility Contracts [official]

axe-core's `axe.configure()` API allows teams to register custom rules that enforce project-specific accessibility contracts not covered by the default ruleset — for example, ensuring that every `<img>` in the product catalogue has a non-empty `alt` attribute drawn from the CMS alt-text field, or that all interactive components have a `data-testid` for AT identification. Custom rules integrate seamlessly with existing `axe.run()` calls and appear in the violations array like any built-in rule.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

// Custom rule: every product card image must have a non-generic alt text
const productImageAltRule = {
  id: 'product-image-alt-text',
  selector: '[data-component="product-card"] img',
  tags: ['custom', 'wcag2a'],
  metadata: {
    description: 'Product card images must have descriptive alt text (not generic)',
    help: 'Provide meaningful alt text drawn from product CMS description',
    helpUrl: 'https://wiki.internal/a11y/product-images',
  },
  any: [
    {
      id: 'product-image-alt-check',
      evaluate(node: Element) {
        const alt = (node as HTMLImageElement).alt;
        if (!alt || alt.length < 5) return false;
        const genericPatterns = /^(image|photo|picture|img|product)$/i;
        return !genericPatterns.test(alt.trim());
      },
    },
  ],
};

test('product cards have descriptive alt text (custom axe rule)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Register the custom rule before running the scan
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    // axe is injected by AxeBuilder; register rule after axe loads
  });

  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .options({
      rules: { 'product-image-alt-text': { enabled: true } },
    })
    .analyze();

  const customViolations = results.violations.filter(
    (v) => v.id === 'product-image-alt-text',
  );
  expect(customViolations).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom axe rules must be registered via `axe.configure()` inside the browser context, which requires injecting the rule definition as a serialisable script rather than passing a TypeScript object directly from the Node.js test process. The `page.addInitScript()` approach shown above requires the rule's `evaluate` function to be stringified — closures over Node.js variables are not available. For complex rules, teams maintain a separate browser-side JS file that is injected via `page.addInitScript({ path: './a11y-custom-rules.js' })`, keeping the rule logic testable independently of Playwright. [official]

---

### Pattern 246 — ARIA `role="feed"` with `aria-busy`: Testing Infinite Scroll Loading State Announcements [official]

The ARIA APG Feed pattern requires the container to have `role="feed"`, each item to have `role="article"` with a unique accessible name, and the container to set `aria-busy="true"` while new content is loading so screen readers can announce "busy" and suppress premature reading of partial content. When infinite scroll triggers a load, `aria-busy` must flip to `true`, then back to `false` once the new articles are appended. Tests must verify the state machine: idle → loading (`aria-busy="true"`) → loaded (`aria-busy="false"`) with new articles present.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('infinite scroll feed sets aria-busy during load and announces new articles', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/news-feed');

  const feed = page.locator('[role="feed"]');
  await expect(feed).toBeVisible();
  await expect(feed).toHaveAttribute('aria-busy', 'false');

  // Count initial articles
  const initialArticles = await page.locator('[role="feed"] [role="article"]').count();
  expect(initialArticles).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  // Each article must have an accessible name
  const articles = await page.locator('[role="feed"] [role="article"]').all();
  for (const article of articles.slice(0, 3)) {
    const label = await article.getAttribute('aria-label') ??
                  await article.getAttribute('aria-labelledby');
    expect(label).toBeTruthy();
  }

  // Scroll to bottom to trigger load
  await page.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, document.body.scrollHeight));

  // aria-busy should flip to true during loading
  await expect(feed).toHaveAttribute('aria-busy', 'true');

  // Wait for loading to complete
  await expect(feed).toHaveAttribute('aria-busy', 'false', { timeout: 10_000 });

  // Verify new articles were appended
  const finalArticles = await page.locator('[role="feed"] [role="article"]').count();
  expect(finalArticles).toBeGreaterThan(initialArticles);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `aria-busy` state transition may be extremely brief (under 100ms for fast network responses), making it flaky to assert in CI. Teams should set a network condition throttle or use `page.route()` to delay API responses during the test to give Playwright a reliable window to observe the `aria-busy="true"` state. The alternative is to not assert the intermediate `aria-busy="true"` state and only verify the final state plus article count — a weaker but more stable assertion. [official]

---

### Pattern 247 — `@testing-library/jest-dom` `toHaveAccessibleName`: Unit-Level Accessible Name Assertions [community]

React Testing Library's `toHaveAccessibleName()` matcher computes the accessible name of a rendered element using the browser's accessible name computation algorithm (proxied through `aria-query` + JSDOM), allowing unit tests to assert that labels, `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, and implicit name derivation (button text content, image alt, etc.) produce the expected accessible name without requiring a full browser. This fills the gap between axe-core integration tests (which catch missing labels but not wrong label values) and manual AT testing.

```typescript
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import { expect, test } from 'vitest';
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';
import { IconButton } from '../components/IconButton';

test('IconButton renders with correct accessible name from aria-label', () => {
  render(<IconButton icon="trash" aria-label="Delete item 42" />);

  const button = screen.getByRole('button');

  // Verify the accessible name is exactly as specified
  expect(button).toHaveAccessibleName('Delete item 42');
});

test('IconButton without aria-label falls back to title attribute', () => {
  render(<IconButton icon="trash" title="Delete item" />);

  const button = screen.getByRole('button');

  // title is a valid but lower-priority accessible name source
  expect(button).toHaveAccessibleName('Delete item');
});

test('linked image has accessible name from alt text', () => {
  render(<a href="/dashboard"><img src="logo.svg" alt="Acme Corp dashboard" /></a>);

  const link = screen.getByRole('link');
  expect(link).toHaveAccessibleName('Acme Corp dashboard');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** JSDOM does not implement the full browser rendering engine, so `toHaveAccessibleName()` can produce different results than a real browser for complex name computations involving CSS (e.g., `::before` pseudo-element content used as visible labels, or `display:none` elements referenced by `aria-labelledby`). For components relying on CSS-generated content for their accessible name, Playwright's `locator.evaluate(() => element.textContent)` or a snapshot test is more reliable. JSDOM-based assertions are fast and suitable for the majority of straightforward naming patterns. [community]

---

### Pattern 248 — Playwright `page.getByRole()` with `level` Option: Asserting Heading Hierarchy [community]

Playwright's `getByRole('heading', { level: N })` locator enforces both the semantic role and the heading level in a single assertion, making it the most concise way to verify that pages use a correct and non-skipped heading hierarchy. Heading hierarchy failures (e.g., jumping from `<h2>` to `<h4>`, or using `<h1>` multiple times) are a common WCAG 1.3.1 failure that axe-core's `heading-order` rule detects at the page level but cannot pinpoint without element-level assertions. Combining `getByRole` heading assertions with an ordered snapshot of all heading levels gives complete structural coverage.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('page heading hierarchy is correct and non-skipped', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/about');

  // Only one H1 must exist
  const h1s = await page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 }).all();
  expect(h1s).toHaveLength(1);
  await expect(h1s[0]).toContainText(/about us|our story/i);

  // Collect all heading levels in DOM order
  const headingLevels = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const headings = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6'));
    return headings.map((h) => parseInt(h.tagName.slice(1), 10));
  });

  // Verify no level is skipped: each step increase must be at most +1
  for (let i = 1; i < headingLevels.length; i++) {
    const prev = headingLevels[i - 1];
    const curr = headingLevels[i];
    if (curr > prev) {
      expect(curr - prev).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1); // no skipping
    }
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The "no skipping" rule applies to nested heading structures but legitimate page designs sometimes intentionally place an `<h4>` after an `<h2>` when the `<h3>` is rendered in a different branch of the layout (e.g., a sidebar). WCAG 1.3.1 does not technically prohibit skipped headings in all contexts — it requires structure to convey information, not that headings follow a strict sequential rule. The test above is stricter than WCAG requires; teams should accept that some pages will need exceptions documented inline, and the `headingLevels` array can be snapshotted to detect regressions rather than enforcing the strict +1 rule. [community]

---

### Pattern 249 — `prefers-reduced-motion` Media Query: Disabling Animation in Playwright Tests [community]

Users with vestibular disorders, epilepsy, or motion sensitivities rely on the `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query to suppress or minimise animations. WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA) and the WCAG 2 Understanding document for 2.3.1 (Three Flashes) both address motion-related harm. Testing in Playwright requires emulating the `prefers-reduced-motion` media feature to verify that CSS animations and JavaScript-driven transitions are disabled or replaced with instant transitions when the user preference is set.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('animated hero banner respects prefers-reduced-motion', async ({ browser }) => {
  // Launch a context with prefers-reduced-motion: reduce
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    reducedMotion: 'reduce',
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();

  await page.goto('/');

  const banner = page.locator('[data-component="hero-banner"]');

  // Verify animation-duration is 0s or animation is none in reduced motion mode
  const animationDuration = await banner.evaluate((el) => {
    return window.getComputedStyle(el).animationDuration;
  });

  // 0s or 0.01s (some libs use tiny non-zero values as "instant")
  const durationMs = parseFloat(animationDuration) * 1000;
  expect(durationMs).toBeLessThanOrEqual(10);

  // Verify auto-advancing carousel is paused
  const autoPlayActive = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const carousel = document.querySelector('[data-carousel]');
    return carousel?.getAttribute('data-auto-play') === 'true';
  });
  expect(autoPlayActive).toBe(false);

  await context.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `browser.newContext({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' })` emulates the CSS media query at the Playwright level, but it does not emulate the operating system's "Reduce Motion" accessibility setting in a way that affects JavaScript APIs like the Web Animations API's `document.getAnimations()`. If an animation is controlled entirely in JavaScript without checking `matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')`, Playwright's `reducedMotion` context option will not suppress it. Teams should test both the CSS layer (computed style) and the JavaScript layer (checking if animations are paused via the Web Animations API or the component's own state). [community]

---

### Pattern 250 — Accessible Error Summary Patterns: Focus Management After Form Validation Failure [community]

When a form fails server-side validation and the page is reloaded or re-rendered, WCAG 3.3.1 (Error Identification) and 3.3.3 (Error Suggestion) require that errors are identified and described. Best practice (and WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order guidance) is to move focus to an error summary at the top of the form so screen reader users are immediately aware that errors occurred. Tests must verify that (a) an error summary exists with role="alert" or as a heading, (b) focus lands on or near the summary after submission, and (c) each error includes a link that focuses the offending field.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form validation: error summary receives focus and links to fields', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/billing');

  // Submit empty required form
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /submit|place order/i }).click();

  // Error summary must appear
  const errorSummary = page.locator('[data-component="error-summary"]');
  await expect(errorSummary).toBeVisible();

  // Summary must have an accessible heading or alert role
  const summaryRole = await errorSummary.getAttribute('role');
  const summaryTag = await errorSummary.evaluate((el) => el.tagName.toLowerCase());
  const isAlertOrHeading =
    summaryRole === 'alert' ||
    summaryRole === 'alertdialog' ||
    ['h1', 'h2', 'h3'].includes(summaryTag);
  expect(isAlertOrHeading).toBe(true);

  // Focus must move to the error summary after submission
  await expect(errorSummary).toBeFocused();

  // Each error link must navigate focus to the offending field
  const errorLinks = await errorSummary.getByRole('link').all();
  expect(errorLinks.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  for (const link of errorLinks.slice(0, 2)) {
    await link.click();
    // The targeted field should now be focused
    const targetId = await link.getAttribute('href'); // e.g., "#card-number"
    if (targetId?.startsWith('#')) {
      const fieldId = targetId.slice(1);
      const field = page.locator(`#${fieldId}`);
      await expect(field).toBeFocused();
    }
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Moving focus programmatically (`element.focus()`) after form submission requires the error summary element to have `tabindex="-1"` — without it, `focus()` calls on non-natively-focusable elements (like a `<div>` or `<h2>`) are silently ignored in most browsers, and focus stays on the submit button. Teams frequently discover this bug only when testing with keyboard or screen reader, because mouse users receive visual feedback that errors appeared regardless of focus position. The Playwright test guards against this by asserting `toBeFocused()` on the summary element; the implementation fix is `<div tabindex="-1" data-component="error-summary">`. [community]

---

### New Community Gotchas (Cycle 51)

231. **[community] `aria-label` on a container element (`<div>`, `<section>`, `<nav>`) is ignored by screen readers unless the element also has a `role` that makes it a landmark or named widget — adding `aria-label="Main content"` to a plain `<div>` produces no announcement because `<div>` has no ARIA role and therefore no accessible name computation is triggered**: Developers add `aria-label` attributes to container `<div>` elements expecting screen readers to announce the label as a region title. Without an explicit `role` (e.g., `role="region"`, `role="group"`, `role="navigation"`), the `aria-label` is present in the DOM but the accessible name algorithm does not fire for that element type. WHY: The accessible name computation specification defines which roles are "nameable" — only elements with roles that accept an accessible name participate in name computation. A `<div>` with no role is a generic container; the AT ignores its label. The fix is to pair `aria-label` with an appropriate role (e.g., `<div role="region" aria-label="Main content">`) or switch to a semantic HTML element (`<section aria-label="Main content">`). [community]

232. **[community] `focusTrap` libraries that use `document.activeElement` polling to detect focus escaping the trap fail silently when the user opens a browser context menu, a browser extension popup, or a native `<dialog>` opened by the browser (e.g., `window.alert()`) — the browser moves focus to its own UI, `document.activeElement` returns `null` or the `<body>`, and the trap library interprets this as a focus escape and forcibly returns focus to the dialog, creating an inescapable focus trap that prevents the user from using browser tools**: This scenario is most common in enterprise applications that use `alert()`, `confirm()`, or browser-native print dialogs while a custom modal is open. WHY: Custom focus trap implementations monitor `blur` or `focusin` events to detect focus leaving the trap boundary, but browser chrome and extension popups do not fire DOM focus events — they silently steal focus at the OS level. The fix is to use the browser-native `<dialog>` element with the `showModal()` method, which automatically manages the focus trap using the browser's own mechanism and correctly handles interactions with browser UI. [community]

233. **[community] `role="presentation"` and `role="none"` on a `<table>` element remove the table's semantic role from the accessibility tree but do NOT remove the roles of the table's child elements (`<tr>`, `<th>`, `<td>`) — screen readers still announce individual cells as "row X, column Y" because the child elements retain their implicit ARIA roles, creating a confusing experience that is worse than either a fully semantic table or a fully presentational layout**: Developers use `<table role="presentation">` for layout tables (a legacy HTML practice), then add `role="none"` expecting the entire table structure to become invisible to AT. The accessibility tree still contains the child cell elements with their row/column semantics. WHY: The ARIA specification requires that `role="none"` removes the element's own role but explicitly states that it does not propagate to descendants. To create a fully presentational table, every `<th>` and `<td>` must also receive `role="none"`, or (better) the layout must be rewritten using CSS Flexbox/Grid with `<div>` elements that have no implicit table semantics. [community]

234. **[community] When a Playwright test clicks a toggle button that shows/hides content and then immediately asserts `aria-expanded="true"`, the assertion can pass even if the component forgot to update `aria-expanded` — because the attribute update and the DOM visibility change happen in the same synchronous JavaScript microtask, and Playwright's auto-waiting resolves as soon as the attribute is present rather than waiting for a specific value**: Teams write `await button.click(); await expect(button).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true')` and see it pass consistently in CI, but the `aria-expanded` attribute was never actually changed — the initial static HTML had `aria-expanded="true"` hard-coded as a default, and the component only toggles content visibility via CSS without updating the attribute. WHY: `toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true')` passes immediately if the attribute already has that value before the click. The robust pattern is to assert the initial state before clicking (`await expect(button).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false')`), click, then assert the toggled state — creating a before/after contract that catches both frozen-attribute bugs and inverted-logic bugs. [community]

235. **[community] Using `tabindex="0"` on every cell of a data grid (`<td tabindex="0">`) violates the roving `tabindex` pattern required by the ARIA Grid pattern and causes the Tab key to visit every single cell in the grid, creating an extremely long tab sequence that keyboard users must navigate through to reach content after the grid — on a 10×20 grid this means 200 Tab presses to move past the table**: The ARIA Grid pattern specifies that the grid itself has `tabindex="0"` and acts as a single tab stop; internal navigation uses Arrow keys. Only the currently active cell gets `tabindex="0"` at any time; all other cells have `tabindex="-1"`. This is the "roving tabindex" pattern. WHY: Developers apply `tabindex="0"` to all cells thinking it makes them "accessible", unaware that this creates a tab-key storm. The correct implementation uses JavaScript to move `tabindex="0"` to the focused cell on Arrow key events and set all others to `tabindex="-1"`. axe-core does not detect this pattern failure because individual `tabindex="0"` cells are technically valid — the failure is architectural, not per-element. [community]
