### Community Gotchas

**G266** — `aria-label` on a container element silently overrides the accessible names of ALL its descendant interactive elements when AT computes the container's subtree name — leading to screen readers announcing parent labels instead of child button names
Why this matters: ARIA's accessible name computation algorithm (accName 1.2) uses "name from content" for container roles. When a `<nav aria-label="Main Navigation">` contains buttons, screen readers correctly scope the label to the nav landmark. However, developers sometimes place `aria-label` on `<div>` or `<section>` elements that have no landmark role — this creates a named container whose name can bleed into AT announcements if the AT uses flat-tree traversal. More critically: adding `aria-label` to a `<button>` that contains a visible text span and an icon SVG correctly overrides the computed name from content, but if the label text does not contain the button's visible text, WCAG 2.5.3 (Label in Name) is violated — voice control users say the visible text to activate the button, and if the accessible name is different (e.g., `aria-label="Close modal"` on a button showing "X"), Dragon NaturallySpeaking cannot activate it.
Fix: Audit every `aria-label` on interactive elements to confirm the visible label text is a substring of the `aria-label` value. Use Playwright: `await expect(button).toHaveAccessibleName(/visible text/i)` combined with a check that the accessible name contains the `textContent`. Run the axe-core `label-content-name-mismatch` rule (`AxeBuilder.withRules(['label-content-name-mismatch'])`) to catch 2.5.3 violations automatically.

**G267** — React `useEffect`-driven focus management that calls `ref.current.focus()` inside a `useEffect` with an empty dependency array fires after every hot-module-reload in development — creating phantom focus-trap violations that only appear in the dev environment
Why this matters: Development teams running Playwright tests against `next dev` or `vite dev` with HMR enabled may observe intermittent focus-trap failures where a modal or dialog appears to trap focus incorrectly. The root cause is that React 18 Strict Mode double-invokes effects in development — `useEffect(() => { ref.current?.focus(); }, [])` fires twice, the second invocation moving focus back into a component that should have been cleaned up. In Playwright, this causes `page.keyboard.press('Escape')` to close the dialog, then focus immediately snaps back into it on the second effect invocation, making the dialog appear to re-open or trap focus. This is invisible in production (effects fire once) but causes systematic test failures in dev-mode CI.
Fix: Always run Playwright accessibility tests against a production build (`next build && next start` or `vite build && vite preview`) or disable Strict Mode for the specific component under test using `<React.StrictMode>` exclusion. Add a comment in your Playwright config: `// NOTE: Run against prod build — HMR Strict Mode double-invoke causes spurious focus failures`. Gate the CI accessibility job on the build artifact, not the dev server.

**G268** — `inert` attribute browser support gap: Safari 15.4 and earlier versions do NOT support the `inert` attribute — falling back to manual `aria-hidden` + `tabindex` management, which is error-prone when dynamic content is injected inside the inert region
Why this matters: The `inert` attribute (now baseline across Chrome 102+, Firefox 112+, Safari 15.5+) is the recommended way to make background content unreachable when a modal is open — it removes elements from tab order, pointer events, and the accessibility tree in a single attribute. However, applications that still target Safari 15.4 (common in enterprise MDM environments) must polyfill `inert` or fall back to the `aria-hidden` + recursive `tabindex="-1"` pattern. The polyfill (`wicg-inert`) has a known issue: dynamically injected DOM nodes inside an inert region are NOT automatically made inert — the polyfill requires a `MutationObserver` to re-apply the inert behavior, but there is a 1-frame window where newly injected content is briefly focusable.
Fix: If targeting Safari < 15.5, use the `wicg-inert` polyfill AND add a MutationObserver in your modal component to re-apply inert to any dynamically injected children. In Playwright, test for the 1-frame race condition by programmatically injecting a button into the inert region immediately after modal open and asserting it is not focusable: `await expect(injectedButton).not.toBeFocused()` after `await page.keyboard.press('Tab')`.

**G269** — `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` in Playwright v1.49+ uses a YAML-based matching format — but snapshot files generated on macOS differ from those generated on Windows due to platform-specific line endings (CRLF vs LF) causing snapshot mismatch failures in cross-platform CI
Why this matters: Playwright's `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` writes `.aria.yml` snapshot files that use YAML multiline block scalars for accessible text content. On Windows, Playwright's snapshot writer uses CRLF line endings by default if the system `os.EOL` is `\r\n`. When the same test runs on a Linux-based CI container, the snapshot comparison uses LF — the byte-level comparison fails even though the semantic content is identical. This is particularly insidious because the diff shows invisible whitespace differences that are hard to diagnose. Teams using mixed macOS/Windows development environments with Linux CI are most affected.
Fix: Configure Playwright to normalize line endings in snapshot files by adding `snapshotPathTemplate: '{testDir}/__snapshots__/{testFilePath}/{arg}{ext}'` and committing a `.gitattributes` rule: `*.aria.yml text eol=lf`. This forces Git to normalize line endings on checkout to LF across all platforms. Alternatively, set `PLAYWRIGHT_ARIA_SNAPSHOT_EOL=lf` in your CI environment variable configuration once Playwright exposes this option (tracked in playwright#33421).

**G270** — axe-core `color-contrast` rule silently skips elements that have `opacity: 0` in a parent ancestor — partially transparent overlays used for skeleton loaders and shimmer effects are not scanned, allowing contrast violations to ship undetected when the component becomes fully visible
Why this matters: Skeleton loaders and shimmer animations commonly use a `<div>` wrapper with `opacity: 0` that transitions to `opacity: 1` when content loads. axe-core's color-contrast computation skips any element whose effective opacity (the product of all ancestor opacity values) is below a threshold — by default, elements with effective opacity < 0.1 are excluded. This is intentional to avoid false positives on hidden content, but it means contrast violations in skeleton states or content that is briefly at opacity < 0.1 during animation are never flagged. If the design uses a light-grey shimmer (`#e0e0e0`) over a near-white background (`#f5f5f5`) the contrast ratio is ~1.2:1 — well below the 3:1 threshold for UI components — but axe never sees it because the element is at opacity 0 when the scan runs.
Fix: After page load, explicitly test skeleton/shimmer components by injecting CSS to force `opacity: 1 !important` on known skeleton containers before running the axe scan: `await page.addStyleTag({ content: '.skeleton, [data-skeleton] { opacity: 1 !important; }' })`. Then run a targeted axe scan on the skeleton region: `new AxeBuilder({ page }).include('.skeleton').withRules(['color-contrast']).analyze()`. Add this as a dedicated test that mocks the loading state (e.g., mock the API to delay response, capture the skeleton DOM, then scan it).

## Cycle 59 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 356** — WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance — validate focus ring area and contrast ratio using Playwright geometry APIs
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('WCAG 2.4.13 focus appearance: ring area ≥ area of 2px perimeter and contrast ≥ 3:1', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  const buttons = page.locator('button, a, [role="button"], input, select, textarea');
  const count   = await buttons.count();

  for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(count, 10); i++) {
    const btn = buttons.nth(i);
    await btn.focus();

    const focusStyle = await btn.evaluate((el) => {
      const cs = getComputedStyle(el);
      return {
        outlineWidth:  parseFloat(cs.outlineWidth),
        outlineOffset: parseFloat(cs.outlineOffset),
        outlineColor:  cs.outlineColor,
        bgColor:       cs.backgroundColor,
      };
    });

    // 2.4.13 requires the focus indicator area ≥ perimeter of the component × 2px
    // A simple proxy: outline-width + outline-offset must be ≥ 2px total
    const indicatorThickness = focusStyle.outlineWidth + focusStyle.outlineOffset;
    expect(
      indicatorThickness,
      `Element index ${i}: focus indicator thickness (outline-width + outline-offset) must be ≥ 2px for WCAG 2.4.13`
    ).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);

    // Verify outline is not "transparent" or "rgba(0,0,0,0)"
    expect(
      focusStyle.outlineColor,
      `Element index ${i}: outline-color must not be transparent`
    ).not.toMatch(/rgba\(0,\s*0,\s*0,\s*0\)/);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: This test measures `outline-width + outline-offset` as a proxy for the WCAG 2.4.13 area requirement, but the actual specification measures the enclosed area of the focus indicator against the perimeter length of the component — a geometry calculation requiring `getBoundingClientRect()` on both the element and its rendered focus ring (which has no direct DOM representation). The proxy is sufficient for CI gating but will miss cases where a very large button has an outline whose area is geometrically insufficient even though the pixel thickness looks correct. For high-fidelity compliance, screenshot the focused element and use pixel-diffing to measure the ring area.

**Pattern 357** — ARIA `role="status"` vs `role="alert"` — verify correct politeness level for dynamic notifications
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('aria-live regions: status uses polite, alert uses assertive, no politeness mismatch', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // 1. Collect all live region elements and verify role/aria-live consistency
  const liveRegions = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const liveEls = Array.from(
      document.querySelectorAll('[aria-live], [role="status"], [role="alert"], [role="log"], [role="timer"]')
    );
    return liveEls.map(el => ({
      tag:       el.tagName.toLowerCase(),
      role:      el.getAttribute('role') ?? '',
      ariaLive:  el.getAttribute('aria-live') ?? '',
      ariaAtomic: el.getAttribute('aria-atomic') ?? '',
      id:        el.id,
    }));
  });

  for (const region of liveRegions) {
    if (region.role === 'alert') {
      // role="alert" has implicit aria-live="assertive" — an explicit polite override is a mismatch
      expect(
        region.ariaLive,
        `role="alert" element (id="${region.id}") must not be overridden with aria-live="polite"`
      ).not.toBe('polite');
    }
    if (region.role === 'status') {
      // role="status" has implicit aria-live="polite" — assertive is a mismatch
      expect(
        region.ariaLive,
        `role="status" element (id="${region.id}") must not be overridden with aria-live="assertive"`
      ).not.toBe('assertive');
    }
  }

  // 2. Confirm axe-core finds no aria-live region rule violations
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withRules(['aria-required-attr', 'aria-allowed-attr', 'aria-valid-attr-value'])
    .analyze();
  expect(results.violations).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: The test checks for explicit `aria-live` attributes that contradict the implicit politeness of `role="alert"` or `role="status"`, but browsers may honour the role's implicit value even when an explicit override is present — making the mismatch a semantic authoring error that not all AT implementations surface as an audible issue. The axe rules checked here (`aria-required-attr`, `aria-allowed-attr`) catch structural problems but do not validate whether the announcement timing actually matches user expectations. Pair this with a real screen reader smoke test (NVDA + Chrome or VoiceOver + Safari) for each live region to validate announcement behaviour.

**Pattern 358** — `aria-describedby` wiring — verify description elements exist and are non-empty for all referencing controls
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('aria-describedby: all referenced description elements exist and contain text', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/form');

  const mismatches: string[] = [];

  const controls = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('[aria-describedby]')).map(el => ({
      tag:         el.tagName.toLowerCase(),
      id:          el.id || '(no id)',
      describedBy: el.getAttribute('aria-describedby') ?? '',
    }));
  });

  for (const ctrl of controls) {
    const ids = ctrl.describedBy.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
    for (const refId of ids) {
      const descEl = page.locator(`#${CSS.escape(refId)}`);
      const exists  = await descEl.count();
      if (exists === 0) {
        mismatches.push(`Control id="${ctrl.id}" references non-existent description id="${refId}"`);
        continue;
      }
      const text = (await descEl.textContent())?.trim() ?? '';
      if (text.length === 0) {
        mismatches.push(`Control id="${ctrl.id}" description id="${refId}" is empty`);
      }
    }
  }

  expect(
    mismatches,
    `aria-describedby wiring issues found:\n${mismatches.join('\n')}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: The `CSS.escape(refId)` call ensures IDs with special characters do not break the locator selector, but this test only verifies that the referenced element exists and has visible text — it does not confirm whether the description text is actually meaningful to a screen reader user. Descriptions that exist but contain only whitespace-only Unicode characters or empty `<span>`s with non-zero computed layout will pass this test. For deeper validation, check `textContent` after stripping zero-width characters: `text.replace(/[​-‍﻿]/g, '').trim()`.

**Pattern 359** — Keyboard shortcut audit — detect single-character key shortcuts (WCAG 2.1.4) without remapping or disable mechanism
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('WCAG 2.1.4: single-char keyboard shortcuts have a disable or remap mechanism', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Collect keydown handlers registered on document/window and interactive elements
  const shortcuts = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const results: Array<{ element: string; key: string }> = [];

    // Check for explicit keydown/keyup attribute handlers on elements
    const els = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('[data-shortcut], [accesskey]'));
    for (const el of els) {
      const key = el.getAttribute('data-shortcut') ?? el.getAttribute('accesskey') ?? '';
      if (key.length === 1) {
        results.push({ element: el.tagName.toLowerCase(), key });
      }
    }

    return results;
  });

  // If any single-char shortcuts exist, verify a preference/settings page exists to disable them
  if (shortcuts.length > 0) {
    const settingsLink = page.locator('a[href*="settings"], a[href*="preferences"], button:has-text("Settings")');
    const settingsCount = await settingsLink.count();
    expect(
      settingsCount,
      `Found single-char shortcuts (${shortcuts.map(s => s.key).join(', ')}) but no settings/preferences UI to disable them — violates WCAG 2.1.4`
    ).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: This test only detects shortcuts declared via `[data-shortcut]` or `[accesskey]` attributes — it will miss shortcuts registered entirely in JavaScript event listeners (the most common pattern in SPAs using libraries like hotkeys-js or mousetrap). A complete WCAG 2.1.4 audit requires manual verification or instrumentation via `page.addInitScript()` to intercept `addEventListener('keydown', ...)` calls on `document` and `window`, capturing the key filter used in each handler. The `accesskey` attribute itself has poor AT support and cross-platform key-combination conflicts, so its presence is itself a flag for review.

**Pattern 360** — `<select>` element accessible name and option group labelling validation
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('select elements: accessible name present, optgroups labelled, axe label rules pass', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/form');

  // 1. Every <select> must have a non-empty accessible name
  const selects = page.locator('select');
  const selectCount = await selects.count();

  for (let i = 0; i < selectCount; i++) {
    const sel = selects.nth(i);
    await expect(sel).toHaveAccessibleName(/.+/);
  }

  // 2. <optgroup> elements must have a non-empty label attribute
  const optgroupsWithoutLabel = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('optgroup:not([label]), optgroup[label=""]'))
      .map(g => `<optgroup> inside <select id="${(g.closest('select') as HTMLSelectElement)?.id}">`)
  });

  expect(
    optgroupsWithoutLabel,
    `Unlabelled <optgroup> elements found: ${optgroupsWithoutLabel.join(', ')}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);

  // 3. Run axe label rules
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withRules(['label', 'select-name'])
    .analyze();
  expect(results.violations).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `toHaveAccessibleName(/.+/)` verifies the name is non-empty but does not verify it is visible to the user — a `<select>` labelled only with `aria-label` is technically accessible but may confuse sighted users who see no visible label. The preferred technique (WCAG 3.3.2) is a visible `<label>` element associated by `for`/`id`. Additionally, native `<select>` elements have severe styling limitations; many teams replace them with custom ARIA comboboxes — if that pattern is used, this test will find no `<select>` elements and the combobox must instead be tested with Pattern 356/combobox contract tests.

**Pattern 361** — Image alt text quality gate — detect alt text that is a filename, dimension string, or stock-photo UUID
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('image alt text quality: no filename, dimension, or UUID-style alt values', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  const badAlts: string[] = [];

  const images = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('img[alt]')).map(img => ({
      src: img.getAttribute('src') ?? '',
      alt: img.getAttribute('alt') ?? '',
    }));
  });

  const filenamePattern  = /\.(png|jpe?g|gif|webp|svg|avif)$/i;
  const dimensionPattern = /^\d+\s*[x×]\s*\d+$/i;
  const uuidPattern      = /^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$/i;
  const tooShortPattern  = /^(img|image|photo|pic|picture|icon|logo)$/i;

  for (const { src, alt } of images) {
    if (alt === '') continue; // empty alt is valid for decorative images
    if (filenamePattern.test(alt))  badAlts.push(`src="${src}" alt="${alt}" — looks like a filename`);
    if (dimensionPattern.test(alt)) badAlts.push(`src="${src}" alt="${alt}" — looks like a dimension string`);
    if (uuidPattern.test(alt))      badAlts.push(`src="${src}" alt="${alt}" — looks like a UUID/asset key`);
    if (tooShortPattern.test(alt))  badAlts.push(`src="${src}" alt="${alt}" — generic/meaningless alt text`);
  }

  expect(
    badAlts,
    `Images with low-quality alt text detected:\n${badAlts.join('\n')}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: Pattern matching on alt text strings is heuristic — it catches common CMS and asset-pipeline failures (where alt is auto-populated from the filename) but will miss alt text that is semantically incorrect yet syntactically "good-looking" (e.g., `alt="decorative swirl"` on an image that actually conveys the product name). The `tooShortPattern` check may produce false positives on legitimate cases like `alt="Logo"` on the site logo (though the preferred pattern is `alt="Acme Inc. logo"`). The most reliable complement is a manual content audit of every non-decorative image's alt text by a content editor familiar with the images.

**Pattern 362** — `prefers-reduced-motion` media query — verify animations are suppressed when user opts in
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('prefers-reduced-motion: animations reduced or removed when preference is active', async ({ page }) => {
  // Emulate reduced-motion preference
  await page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' });
  await page.goto('/');

  // 1. Verify no CSS transitions or animations run on key animated elements
  const animatedElements = page.locator('[class*="animate"], [class*="transition"], [class*="spin"], [class*="fade"]');
  const count = await animatedElements.count();

  for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(count, 15); i++) {
    const el = animatedElements.nth(i);
    const styles = await el.evaluate((node) => {
      const cs = getComputedStyle(node);
      return {
        animationName:     cs.animationName,
        animationDuration: cs.animationDuration,
        transitionDuration: cs.transitionDuration,
      };
    });

    const hasAnimation = styles.animationName !== 'none' && styles.animationDuration !== '0s';
    const hasTransition = styles.transitionDuration !== '0s';

    if (hasAnimation || hasTransition) {
      // Warn — some transitions (e.g., focus ring appearance) are acceptable under reduced-motion
      console.warn(`[reduced-motion] Element index ${i} still has animation/transition: ${JSON.stringify(styles)}`);
    }
  }

  // 2. Axe scan — no new violations introduced in reduced-motion state
  const { violations } = await (await import('@axe-core/playwright')).default.bind(null)({ page } as any);
  // Use direct import pattern for this check
  expect(true).toBe(true); // placeholder — actual axe call in full implementation
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' })` only affects media queries in CSS — it does not pause JavaScript-driven animations that use `requestAnimationFrame` or Web Animations API without checking `window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')`. Libraries like Framer Motion, GSAP, and Lottie require explicit reduced-motion handling in application code. The console.warn approach in step 1 is non-blocking — to make this a hard gate, replace it with `expect(hasAnimation || hasTransition, '...').toBe(false)`. Be careful: legitimate micro-animations such as focus ring fade-in at 100ms are acceptable under WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA) and the `prefers-reduced-motion` preference is advisory, not a hard prohibition on all motion.

**Pattern 363** — Table accessibility — `scope`, `headers`, and `aria-sort` lifecycle validation
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('data table: scope/headers attributes correct, aria-sort updates on column sort click', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/data-table');

  // 1. Every th must have scope="col" or scope="row" (or use headers on td)
  const thWithoutScope = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('table th'))
      .filter(th => !th.getAttribute('scope') && !th.getAttribute('id'))
      .map(th => th.textContent?.trim() ?? '(empty)');
  });
  expect(thWithoutScope, `<th> elements missing scope attribute: ${thWithoutScope.join(', ')}`).toHaveLength(0);

  // 2. If sortable columns exist, aria-sort must be "ascending", "descending", or "none" (not absent)
  const sortableHeaders = page.locator('th[aria-sort], th button[aria-sort]');
  const sortCount = await sortableHeaders.count();

  if (sortCount > 0) {
    const firstSortable = page.locator('th[aria-sort]').first();
    const initialSort = await firstSortable.getAttribute('aria-sort');
    expect(['ascending', 'descending', 'none']).toContain(initialSort);

    // Click to sort and verify aria-sort changes
    await firstSortable.click();
    await page.waitForTimeout(200); // allow sort animation
    const afterSort = await firstSortable.getAttribute('aria-sort');
    expect(afterSort).not.toBe(initialSort);
    expect(['ascending', 'descending', 'none']).toContain(afterSort);
  }

  // 3. Axe table rules
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withRules(['td-headers-attr', 'th-has-data-cells', 'scope-attr-valid', 'table-duplicate-name'])
    .analyze();
  expect(results.violations).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: The `aria-sort` click test relies on a 200ms `waitForTimeout` for the sort state to update — this is fragile if the sort is async (fetches from API). Replace with `await page.waitForFunction(() => document.querySelector('th[aria-sort]')?.getAttribute('aria-sort') !== 'none')` for a more reliable wait. The `scope` check requires all `<th>` to have a `scope` or `id` attribute — complex tables using the `headers` attribute on `<td>` elements (where individual cells reference multiple header IDs) are a legitimate alternative that this test does not validate; add a separate pass checking that all `headers` attribute values resolve to existing `id` values.

**Pattern 364** — Custom `role="listbox"` keyboard contract — ArrowUp/Down selection, Home/End, typeahead
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('role="listbox": ArrowUp/Down, Home/End keyboard navigation and aria-selected updates', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/custom-select');

  const listbox = page.locator('[role="listbox"]');
  await expect(listbox).toBeVisible();
  await listbox.focus();

  const options = listbox.locator('[role="option"]');
  const optCount = await options.count();
  expect(optCount).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  // 1. ArrowDown moves aria-activedescendant to first option
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowDown');
  const activeId = await listbox.getAttribute('aria-activedescendant');
  expect(activeId).toBeTruthy();

  // 2. First active option has aria-selected="true"
  const firstActive = page.locator(`#${activeId}`);
  await expect(firstActive).toHaveAttribute('aria-selected', 'true');

  // 3. ArrowDown again moves to second option
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowDown');
  const activeId2 = await listbox.getAttribute('aria-activedescendant');
  expect(activeId2).not.toBe(activeId);

  // 4. Home key returns to first option
  await page.keyboard.press('Home');
  const activeIdHome = await listbox.getAttribute('aria-activedescendant');
  const firstOptionId = await options.first().getAttribute('id');
  expect(activeIdHome).toBe(firstOptionId);

  // 5. End key moves to last option
  await page.keyboard.press('End');
  const activeIdEnd = await listbox.getAttribute('aria-activedescendant');
  const lastOptionId = await options.last().getAttribute('id');
  expect(activeIdEnd).toBe(lastOptionId);
});
```
Tradeoff: The test assumes the listbox uses the `aria-activedescendant` pattern — where the listbox itself holds focus and `aria-activedescendant` points to the active option. Some listbox implementations use the roving-tabindex pattern instead (focus physically moves to each `[role="option"]`). In that case, `aria-activedescendant` will always be null and the test will fail with a false negative. Before running this test, verify which focus management pattern the component uses. Also note that the ARIA APG recommends `aria-selected` to track selection (persistent) separately from `aria-current` or `aria-activedescendant` for navigation focus — mixing these concepts is a common authoring error.

**Pattern 365** — `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` integrity check for disclosure widgets
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('disclosure widgets: aria-expanded toggles correctly and aria-controls references exist', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  const triggers = page.locator('[aria-expanded][aria-controls]');
  const count = await triggers.count();

  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const trigger  = triggers.nth(i);
    const controls = await trigger.getAttribute('aria-controls');
    const expanded = await trigger.getAttribute('aria-expanded');

    // Verify the controlled element exists
    const controlledEl = page.locator(`#${controls}`);
    await expect(controlledEl.first()).toBeAttached();

    // Verify expanded state is boolean string
    expect(['true', 'false']).toContain(expanded);

    // Click to toggle
    await trigger.click();
    const expandedAfter = await trigger.getAttribute('aria-expanded');
    expect(expandedAfter).not.toBe(expanded); // must toggle

    // The controlled panel visibility must match aria-expanded
    const isVisible = await controlledEl.first().isVisible();
    expect(isVisible).toBe(expandedAfter === 'true');

    // Restore original state
    await trigger.click();
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: The test assumes a direct click on the trigger toggles `aria-expanded` — this is true for simple disclosure buttons but may not hold for accordion implementations that use a controlled component pattern where expand/collapse is driven by external state (e.g., Redux/Zustand). In those cases the click may have a side effect delay due to state update cycles. Add an explicit `await expect(trigger).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', expandedAfter === 'true' ? 'false' : 'true')` after the restore click rather than assuming it resets. Additionally, `aria-controls` is weakly supported by some screen readers (VoiceOver on macOS largely ignores it) — the more robust approach is to also verify that the panel is a DOM sibling or direct child of the trigger's container, which most AT implementations handle correctly by proximity.

**Pattern 366** — Skip navigation link — existence, visibility on focus, and target focusability
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('skip navigation link: present, visible on focus, target is focusable', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // 1. A skip link must be the first or near-first focusable element
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
  const focused = page.locator(':focus');
  const href    = await focused.getAttribute('href');
  const text    = (await focused.textContent())?.toLowerCase() ?? '';

  expect(
    text,
    'First Tab stop must be a skip navigation link'
  ).toMatch(/skip|jump|main content/i);

  // 2. Skip link must be visible when focused
  await expect(focused).toBeVisible();

  // 3. Pressing Enter must move focus to the target element
  const targetId = href?.replace('#', '') ?? '';
  await focused.press('Enter');
  const targetEl = page.locator(`#${CSS.escape(targetId)}`);
  await expect(targetEl).toBeFocused();

  // 4. Target must have tabindex="-1" or be a naturally focusable element
  const tabindex = await targetEl.getAttribute('tabindex');
  const tagName  = await targetEl.evaluate(el => el.tagName.toLowerCase());
  const naturallyFocusable = ['a', 'button', 'input', 'select', 'textarea'].includes(tagName);
  const hasMinus1 = tabindex === '-1';
  expect(
    naturallyFocusable || hasMinus1,
    `Skip link target #${targetId} must be focusable (tabindex="-1" or naturally focusable element)`
  ).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: The test assumes the skip link is the absolute first Tab stop. Some designs intentionally place a cookie-consent banner or global announcement before the skip link — this will cause the test to fail even though the skip link is present. A more resilient approach is to Tab up to 5 times and check whether any of the focusable elements in that sequence matches the skip-link pattern. The `focused.press('Enter')` step tests that the anchor activates on Enter; `<button>` skip links activated by Space also need a separate Space keypress test. Finally, `tabindex="-1"` on the target is required for programmatic focus to work in browsers that do not natively focus `<main>` or `<div>` elements — missing this is a common implementation oversight.

**Pattern 367** — `@axe-core/playwright` scan with violation fingerprinting to suppress accepted third-party issues
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';
import { createHash } from 'crypto';

// Known accepted violations from third-party embeds (e.g., chat widget, payment iframe)
// Each fingerprint = SHA-256 of "ruleId|targetSelector"
const ACCEPTED_VIOLATION_FINGERPRINTS = new Set([
  'a3f9c1e2...', // color-contrast | #intercom-iframe
  'b7d4a0f1...', // frame-title    | #stripe-payment-frame
]);

function fingerprintViolation(v: { id: string; nodes: Array<{ target: unknown[] }> }): string {
  const target = JSON.stringify(v.nodes[0]?.target ?? []);
  return createHash('sha256').update(`${v.id}|${target}`).digest('hex').slice(0, 8) + '...';
}

test('axe full-page scan with accepted-violation filtering', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21aa', 'wcag22aa'])
    .analyze();

  const unacceptedViolations = results.violations.filter(v => {
    const fp = fingerprintViolation(v);
    return !ACCEPTED_VIOLATION_FINGERPRINTS.has(fp);
  });

  expect(
    unacceptedViolations.map(v => `[${v.id}] ${v.help} — ${v.nodes.length} node(s)`),
    'Unexpected axe violations found'
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: Fingerprinting using the first node's target selector is fragile — if the third-party embed changes its internal DOM structure (e.g., a chat widget updates its iframe ID), the fingerprint changes and the violation will suddenly re-appear as unaccepted. The fingerprint list requires active maintenance on every third-party version bump. A more durable approach is to exclude third-party iframes by origin using `AxeBuilder.exclude(['#intercom-iframe', '#stripe-payment-frame'])` — this excludes the entire subtree, not just a specific rule. Use fingerprinting only for same-origin components with accepted technical debt where full exclusion would hide other violations in the same DOM region.

**Pattern 368** — `aria-required` and `aria-invalid` lifecycle — form field validation state management
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form validation: aria-required present, aria-invalid transitions on submit attempt', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/form');

  // 1. Required fields must have aria-required="true" or the native required attribute
  const requiredFields = page.locator('input[required], textarea[required], select[required], [aria-required="true"]');
  const count = await requiredFields.count();
  expect(count).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const field = requiredFields.nth(i);
    // Must have accessible name (label)
    await expect(field).toHaveAccessibleName(/.+/);
  }

  // 2. Submit empty form — all required fields should transition to aria-invalid="true"
  const submitBtn = page.locator('button[type="submit"], input[type="submit"]').first();
  await submitBtn.click();

  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const field     = requiredFields.nth(i);
    const tagName   = await field.evaluate(el => el.tagName.toLowerCase());

    // Native validation state OR explicit aria-invalid
    const ariaInvalid = await field.getAttribute('aria-invalid');
    const validity    = await field.evaluate((el) => (el as HTMLInputElement).validity?.valueMissing ?? false);
    const isInvalid   = ariaInvalid === 'true' || validity;
    expect(isInvalid, `Required field index ${i} (${tagName}) must be marked invalid after empty submit`).toBe(true);
  }

  // 3. Fill a field and verify aria-invalid clears
  const firstField = requiredFields.first();
  await firstField.fill('Test value');
  await firstField.blur();
  const ariaInvalidAfter = await firstField.getAttribute('aria-invalid');
  expect(['false', null]).toContain(ariaInvalidAfter);
});
```
Tradeoff: Relying on `validity.valueMissing` tests the native HTML5 constraint validation API, which is only meaningful for native `<input>`, `<textarea>`, and `<select>` elements. Custom components built with `role="textbox"` or `role="combobox"` do not have a `validity` object — for those, `aria-invalid` is the only semantic signal. Additionally, forms that use JavaScript-driven validation (React Hook Form, Zod, Yup) may not set `aria-invalid` synchronously on submit — add `await page.waitForFunction(() => document.querySelector('[aria-required="true"]')?.getAttribute('aria-invalid') === 'true')` to handle async validation state updates.

**Pattern 369** — Heading hierarchy snapshot regression — detect inserted `<h1>` duplicates or skipped heading levels
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('heading hierarchy: single h1, no skipped levels, snapshot regression', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  const headings = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6')).map(h => ({
      level: parseInt(h.tagName[1]),
      text:  h.textContent?.trim().slice(0, 60) ?? '',
    }));
  });

  // 1. Exactly one h1
  const h1s = headings.filter(h => h.level === 1);
  expect(h1s, `Expected exactly 1 <h1>, found ${h1s.length}: ${h1s.map(h => h.text).join(', ')}`).toHaveLength(1);

  // 2. No skipped heading levels (e.g., h1 directly followed by h3)
  for (let i = 1; i < headings.length; i++) {
    const prev = headings[i - 1];
    const curr = headings[i];
    const levelJump = curr.level - prev.level;
    expect(
      levelJump,
      `Heading level skipped: h${prev.level} ("${prev.text}") → h${curr.level} ("${curr.text}")`
    ).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1);
  }

  // 3. Snapshot the heading structure for regression detection
  const headingStructure = headings.map(h => `${'  '.repeat(h.level - 1)}H${h.level}: ${h.text}`).join('\n');
  expect(headingStructure).toMatchSnapshot('heading-hierarchy.txt');
});
```
Tradeoff: The no-skipped-levels rule (`levelJump <= 1`) correctly flags `h1` → `h3` jumps but the reverse direction (going from `h3` back up to `h1` after a section ends) is intentional and valid in HTML — an `h1` can follow an `h6` without violating the heading hierarchy because each heading starts a new section. The test would incorrectly pass a descending-jump scenario. To be fully correct, validate that no heading level increases by more than 1 in the descending direction (level increases) while allowing any decrease. The snapshot approach also requires `--update-snapshots` on first run and on every intentional heading structure change — add a comment in the test file to explain that snapshot updates are expected on page restructuring.

**Pattern 370** — `role="tooltip"` — verify trigger association, keyboard accessibility, and Escape dismissal
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('tooltip: aria-describedby wired, visible on focus, dismissable with Escape', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Find all tooltip triggers
  const triggers = page.locator('[aria-describedby]').filter({
    has: page.locator('[role="tooltip"]')
  });

  // Alternative: find elements whose describedby target has role="tooltip"
  const tooltipTargets = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('[role="tooltip"]')).map(tt => ({
      id:   tt.id,
      text: tt.textContent?.trim() ?? '',
    }));
  });

  for (const tooltip of tooltipTargets) {
    if (!tooltip.id) continue;

    const trigger = page.locator(`[aria-describedby~="${tooltip.id}"]`).first();
    const triggerCount = await trigger.count();
    if (triggerCount === 0) continue;

    // 1. Tab to the trigger and verify tooltip becomes visible
    await trigger.focus();
    const tooltipEl = page.locator(`#${CSS.escape(tooltip.id)}`);
    await expect(tooltipEl).toBeVisible({ timeout: 1000 });

    // 2. Escape must dismiss the tooltip
    await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
    await expect(tooltipEl).toBeHidden({ timeout: 1000 });

    // 3. Tooltip must reappear on re-focus
    await trigger.focus();
    await expect(tooltipEl).toBeVisible({ timeout: 1000 });

    // 4. Pointer can move to the tooltip without it disappearing (WCAG 1.4.13)
    await tooltipEl.hover();
    await expect(tooltipEl).toBeVisible();
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: This test only finds tooltip triggers that use `aria-describedby` pointing to an element with `role="tooltip"` — it will miss tooltip patterns that use `title` attributes (which are inaccessible for keyboard and touch users and should be avoided), `aria-label` overrides without a visible tooltip element, or hover-only custom tooltips without any ARIA association. The Escape dismissal check (`toBeHidden` within 1000ms) assumes the tooltip implementation listens for the `keydown` event on the trigger — some implementations only dismiss on `keyup`. If the tooltip is part of a Radix UI or Floating UI component, it may animate out over 200–300ms, requiring the `timeout` value to account for the exit animation duration.

### Community Gotchas

**G271** — `aria-hidden="true"` on a focusable element does not prevent keyboard focus — the element is hidden from the accessibility tree but Tab still lands on it, leaving keyboard users stranded on an invisible element
Why this matters: `aria-hidden="true"` removes an element from the accessibility tree (screen readers skip it) but browsers do not remove it from the tab order. A common mistake is placing `aria-hidden` on an icon button or SVG link inside a navigation bar to "silence" the icon, while the parent button or anchor remains focusable. When a keyboard user tabs to the element, focus lands on it but the screen reader announces nothing — because the entire element is aria-hidden. Users with visual impairments relying on both keyboard and screen reader are completely stranded: they cannot tell what is focused. This pattern violates WCAG 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) because the element has no accessible name or role in the tree while still being interactive.
Fix: Never place `aria-hidden="true"` on an element that can receive keyboard focus (buttons, links, inputs, or anything with `tabindex >= 0`). Instead: (a) hide the decorative icon inside the button with `aria-hidden`, keeping the button itself visible to AT and providing a text label on the button; (b) or use `tabindex="-1"` alongside `aria-hidden` only if the element is genuinely inert. Audit with Playwright: `await expect(page.locator('[aria-hidden="true"]').filter({ has: page.locator(':focus') })).toHaveCount(0)` — run after tabbing through all interactive elements.

**G272** — `placeholder` attribute text styled with insufficient contrast (< 4.5:1) is a WCAG 1.4.3 violation but axe-core's `color-contrast` rule does not check placeholder text contrast by default — violations ship silently
Why this matters: The CSS `::placeholder` pseudo-element applies a browser-default color of approximately `rgba(0,0,0,0.54)` on a white background, yielding a contrast ratio of ~3.5:1 — below the 4.5:1 requirement for normal text. Design systems frequently customize placeholder color to a light gray (`#999999` on `#FFFFFF` = 2.85:1 ratio) for aesthetic reasons. axe-core's `color-contrast` rule skips `::placeholder` text because the pseudo-element's computed color is not accessible via `getComputedStyle` in the same way as real content — axe reads the element's `color` property, not the `::placeholder` color. The result: placeholder contrast violations are systematically invisible to automated scanning.
Fix: Add a dedicated placeholder contrast test using `page.evaluate` to read `getComputedStyle(input, '::placeholder').color` and compute the contrast ratio against the background: `const ratio = computeContrastRatio(parseRGB(placeholderColor), parseRGB(bgColor)); expect(ratio).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(4.5)`. Alternatively, use the browser DevTools accessibility panel or the axe DevTools Pro extension which includes an experimental `color-contrast` enhancement for pseudo-elements. Update the design system color token for `--placeholder-color` to `#767676` minimum (4.54:1 on white).

**G273** — Infinite scroll and `aria-setsize`/`aria-posinset` — failing to update these attributes as new items load causes screen reader users to hear incorrect position announcements (e.g., "item 10 of 10" when 200 items are eventually available)
Why this matters: Screen readers use `aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` on `[role="listitem"]`, `[role="option"]`, or `[role="row"]` to announce position within a set (e.g., "item 3 of 50"). In infinite scroll implementations, the total item count is either unknown at load time or grows as the user scrolls. Setting `aria-setsize="-1"` correctly communicates "unknown total size" to AT — but many implementations either (a) omit both attributes entirely (leaving AT to count DOM nodes, which is slow and often wrong), (b) set `aria-setsize` to the initial batch size and never update it, or (c) set `aria-setsize` to a hardcoded maximum. All three approaches cause incorrect or misleading announcements. The worst case is `aria-setsize="10"` when 200 items eventually load — users navigating by Arrow keys hear "item 10 of 10" after the 10th item and assume the list has ended.
Fix: For unknown totals, set `aria-setsize="-1"` on all items. If the total is known (e.g., from a paginated API that returns `total_count`), dynamically update `aria-setsize` on all rendered items whenever a new batch loads. In React: use a `useEffect` that updates the attribute on every item in the DOM when `items.length` changes. Test with Playwright: after triggering a scroll-load, verify `aria-setsize` on the last rendered item matches the current `items.length` or is `-1`.

**G274** — `role="presentation"` and `role="none"` on elements with focusable children cause the children to lose their inherited ARIA role context — screen readers may announce the children without their expected landmark or table context
Why this matters: `role="presentation"` (synonym: `role="none"`) removes the semantic role of an element from the accessibility tree but does not propagate to its children — children retain their own roles. The conflict arises in table-based layouts: `<table role="presentation">` is the correct technique for using a `<table>` purely for layout (removing table semantics), and `<td>` children of a presentation table correctly inherit "no table context". However, developers sometimes mistakenly apply `role="presentation"` to `<ul>` elements containing `<li>` items that are navigation links — this removes the list semantics but leaves the `<li>` items without their "listitem" role context, causing VoiceOver to announce each item without the "list, N items" preamble that helps users understand scope. More critically: applying `role="none"` to a focusable element (a `<button>` or `<a>`) is prohibited by ARIA — the role is ignored by browsers for focusable elements.
Fix: Never apply `role="none"` or `role="presentation"` to focusable elements. For navigation `<ul>` elements, preserve the list semantics; if the visual bullet points are unwanted, use CSS `list-style: none` — note that Safari VoiceOver removes list semantics for `list-style: none` lists, requiring `role="list"` to be explicitly re-added. Audit with axe-core rule `presentation-role-conflict` which catches prohibited uses of `role="none"` on focusable elements.

**G275** — `<iframe>` elements without a `title` attribute cause screen reader users to enter an unlabelled frame — users cannot determine the frame's purpose before entering it, leading to disorientation in multi-frame layouts
Why this matters: WCAG 4.1.2 requires all UI components to have a programmatic name. `<iframe>` elements are UI components and must have a `title` attribute that describes the frame's content or purpose (e.g., `title="Payment form"`, `title="Embedded video: Product demo"`). Without a `title`, screen readers announce the frame as "frame" or — in some browsers — read the `src` URL path, which is meaningless to users (`"frame, /assets/widgets/v2/container.html"`). This is particularly common with third-party embeds (Typeform, HubSpot, Intercom, Google Maps) where the third-party provides an embed snippet without a `title`. The axe rule `frame-title` catches missing titles, but the rule is sometimes disabled in configurations that also disable `frame-tested`, causing both rules to be silenced together.
Fix: Always add a descriptive `title` attribute to every `<iframe>` in your codebase. For third-party embeds where the snippet omits a title, add it to the embed code before deployment. For programmatically injected iframes (e.g., Intercom chat widget), use a `MutationObserver` to detect when the iframe is added and set the title: `observer.observe(document.body, { childList: true, subtree: true })` — when an iframe without a title is detected, call `iframe.setAttribute('title', 'Customer support chat')`. Test with Playwright: `await expect(page.locator('iframe:not([title])')).toHaveCount(0)`.

## Cycle 60 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 370** — Axe Full-Page Scan with WCAG 2.2 AA Tag Filter
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('full-page WCAG 2.2 AA scan', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa', 'wcag22aa'])
    .analyze();
  expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
});
```
Tradeoff: Adding `wcag22aa` alongside `wcag21aa` activates WCAG 2.2-specific axe rules (e.g. `target-size`, `focus-not-obscured`) which may fire false positives on inline text links that are exempt from 2.5.8 target-size requirements — exempt link text must be filtered via `.exclude()` or a per-rule `options.xpath` suppression to avoid masking genuine violations with noise.

**Pattern 371** — Violation Fingerprinting to Suppress Accepted Third-Party Issues
```typescript
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const ACCEPTED_VIOLATIONS: Array<{ id: string; target: string }> = [
  { id: 'color-contrast', target: '.third-party-chat-widget' },
];

test('scan with accepted violation suppression', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  const { violations } = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa'])
    .analyze();
  const unexpected = violations.filter(v =>
    !ACCEPTED_VIOLATIONS.some(
      a => a.id === v.id && v.nodes.every(n => n.target.join(' ').includes(a.target))
    )
  );
  expect(unexpected, JSON.stringify(unexpected, null, 2)).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: Fingerprinting by `id + CSS target` is brittle if the third-party widget updates its internal class names — the accepted entry silently fails to match and the violation resurfaces in reports, creating alert fatigue; pin the third-party version in `package-lock.json` and re-audit fingerprints on each upgrade.

**Pattern 372** — WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size Minimum Geometry Check
```typescript
test('interactive targets meet WCAG 2.5.8 24×24 px minimum', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/nav');
  const targets = page.locator('button, a, [role="button"], [role="link"]');
  const count = await targets.count();
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const box = await targets.nth(i).boundingBox();
    if (!box) continue;
    // WCAG 2.5.8: 24×24 CSS px minimum OR 24px spacing offset on all sides
    const meetsSize = box.width >= 24 && box.height >= 24;
    expect(meetsSize, `Target at index ${i} (${box.width}×${box.height}) is below 24×24`).toBe(true);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: This check validates the bounding-box dimension but not the spacing-offset exception in WCAG 2.5.8 — a 16×16 icon link surrounded by ≥24px of empty space on all sides is technically compliant, so naive bounding-box failures will be false positives for tightly-spaced icon grids that rely on the spacing exception; add a neighbour-offset check via `page.evaluate` to honour the full success criterion.

**Pattern 373** — WCAG 1.4.12 Text Spacing Override Reflow Test
```typescript
test('content survives WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing overrides', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/article');
  await page.addStyleTag({
    content: `* {
      line-height: 1.5 !important;
      letter-spacing: 0.12em !important;
      word-spacing: 0.16em !important;
    }
    p { margin-bottom: 2em !important; }`,
  });
  // No content should overflow its container or be clipped
  const clipped = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('p, li, label, td'))
      .filter(el => el.scrollHeight > el.clientHeight + 2)
      .map(el => el.tagName + (el.id ? `#${el.id}` : ''));
  });
  expect(clipped).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: The `scrollHeight > clientHeight` heuristic detects vertical overflow clipping but misses horizontal truncation (e.g. `text-overflow: ellipsis` on single-line headings) and false-positives on elements that are intentionally scrollable — add an `overflow` computed-style guard and exclude elements with `data-scrollable` or an established scroll container role.

**Pattern 374** — WCAG 1.4.13 Hover Content Persistence Test (Tooltip)
```typescript
test('tooltips satisfy WCAG 1.4.13 — hoverable, dismissible, persistent', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/components/tooltip');
  const trigger = page.getByRole('button', { name: /info/i });
  await trigger.hover();
  const tooltip = page.locator('[role="tooltip"]').first();
  await expect(tooltip).toBeVisible();
  // 1. Pointer can enter tooltip without it disappearing
  await tooltip.hover();
  await expect(tooltip).toBeVisible();
  // 2. Escape dismisses the tooltip
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(tooltip).toBeHidden();
  // 3. Tooltip reappears after re-hover
  await trigger.hover();
  await expect(tooltip).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `hover()` in Playwright dispatches `mouseover`/`mouseenter` events but does not simulate the operating-system hover delay — implementations that add a 300ms CSS `transition-delay` before showing the tooltip may cause the `toBeVisible()` assertion to time out at default `timeout: 5000ms`; set an explicit `timeout: 6000` or increase `actionTimeout` in `playwright.config.ts` when testing delayed-show tooltip libraries.

**Pattern 375** — ARIA Snapshot Regression for Dialog Keyboard Contract
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('modal dialog aria snapshot stays stable', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/components/modal');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open modal' }).click();
  const dialog = page.getByRole('dialog');
  await expect(dialog).toBeVisible();
  await expect(dialog).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - dialog "Confirm action":
      - heading "Confirm action" [level=2]
      - paragraph: /Are you sure/
      - button "Cancel"
      - button "Confirm"
  `);
  // Escape must close
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(dialog).toBeHidden();
});
```
Tradeoff: `toMatchAriaSnapshot` uses YAML fragment matching introduced in Playwright 1.49 — the pattern matches a subset of the actual tree so new children added inside the dialog do not break the test, but renamed buttons or changed heading levels will cause failures that require intentional snapshot updates; store snapshots in `__snapshots__` and review diffs in PR as part of the design-change workflow.

**Pattern 376** — WCAG 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication — Paste and Autocomplete Validation
```typescript
test('login form permits paste and autocomplete on credential fields', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  const emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email');
  const passwordInput = page.getByLabel('Password');
  // WCAG 3.3.8: must not block paste — verify field accepts programmatic fill
  await emailInput.fill('user@example.com');
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveValue('user@example.com');
  // Clear and verify paste simulation via fill (clipboard API substitute)
  await emailInput.fill('');
  await emailInput.fill('pasted@example.com');
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveValue('pasted@example.com');
  // Must expose correct autocomplete tokens
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAttribute('autocomplete', 'email');
  await expect(passwordInput).toHaveAttribute('autocomplete', /current-password|new-password/);
});
```
Tradeoff: Playwright's `fill()` bypasses `paste` event handlers that may block clipboard input — to confirm a form does not intercept the `paste` event, dispatch it explicitly with `page.evaluate(() => document.querySelector('input[type=email]')?.dispatchEvent(new ClipboardEvent('paste', { bubbles: true })))` and then check whether the field's `input` event fires normally; also separately verify `autocomplete` attribute values for the semantic WCAG 1.3.5 requirement.

**Pattern 377** — WCAG 3.2.6 Consistent Help — Verify Help Mechanism DOM Order Cross-Page
```typescript
test('help mechanism appears in consistent DOM order on all pages', async ({ page }) => {
  const pages = ['/home', '/account', '/settings'];
  const helpSelectors: number[] = [];
  for (const url of pages) {
    await page.goto(url);
    const position = await page.evaluate(() => {
      const help = document.querySelector('[aria-label*="help" i], a[href*="support" i]');
      if (!help) return -1;
      const all = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('a, button'));
      return all.indexOf(help as HTMLElement);
    });
    helpSelectors.push(position);
    expect(position, `Help not found on ${url}`).toBeGreaterThan(-1);
  }
  // Help should appear in the same relative position block (header or footer)
  const allInHeader = helpSelectors.every(p => p < 20);
  const allInFooter = helpSelectors.every(p => p > 50);
  expect(allInHeader || allInFooter).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: Position-index comparison is a rough proxy for "consistent location" — the WCAG 3.2.6 requirement is about relative location within page structure (header vs. footer), not absolute DOM index; a more robust test uses landmark membership (`page.locator('header').locator('[aria-label*="help"]')`) to verify the help element is inside the same landmark region across all tested pages.

**Pattern 378** — axe `resultTypes` Performance Optimisation for Large Page Scans
```typescript
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('fast axe scan — violations only', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/product-listing?count=500');
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa'])
    .options({ resultTypes: ['violations'] } as never)
    .analyze();
  // Only violations are populated; passes/incomplete are empty arrays
  expect(results.violations).toHaveLength(0);
  expect(results.passes).toHaveLength(0); // not computed
});
```
Tradeoff: `resultTypes: ['violations']` instructs axe-core to skip computing the `passes` and `incomplete` arrays, reducing analysis time by up to 8× on pages with hundreds of DOM nodes — the tradeoff is that you lose `incomplete` (needs-review) results which surface potential violations axe cannot automatically determine (e.g., colour contrast on dynamically computed backgrounds); run a nightly full scan with `resultTypes: ['violations','incomplete']` for comprehensive coverage.

**Pattern 379** — WCAG 1.3.4 Orientation Lock Detection Test
```typescript
test('content is not locked to portrait orientation', async ({ browser }) => {
  // Simulate landscape viewport
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    viewport: { width: 844, height: 390 },
    isMobile: true,
    hasTouch: true,
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  // Page should render meaningful content — not an orientation-lock overlay
  const lockOverlay = page.locator('[class*="orientation"], [class*="rotate-device"]');
  await expect(lockOverlay).toHaveCount(0);
  // Main content area should be visible
  await expect(page.locator('main, [role="main"]')).toBeVisible();
  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: CSS `@media (orientation: landscape)` overlays that use `display: none` to hide the main content will be correctly caught by `toBeVisible()` — but JavaScript-driven orientation locks that display a full-screen overlay element (rather than hiding `<main>`) require an additional check for elements with `z-index > 9000` covering the viewport, which must be implemented via `page.evaluate` geometry comparisons.

**Pattern 380** — WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose — Autocomplete Attribute Audit
```typescript
test('personal data inputs expose correct autocomplete tokens', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  const fieldMap: Array<[string, string]> = [
    ['First name',    'given-name'],
    ['Last name',     'family-name'],
    ['Email',         'email'],
    ['Phone',         'tel'],
    ['Street address','street-address'],
    ['Postal code',   'postal-code'],
    ['Country',       'country'],
  ];
  for (const [label, token] of fieldMap) {
    const input = page.getByLabel(label);
    if (await input.count() === 0) continue;
    await expect(input).toHaveAttribute('autocomplete', token);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `getByLabel` relies on a visible `<label>` element or `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` association — inputs that rely solely on `placeholder` as a visible label have no accessible name and will fail `getByLabel` lookup, which means this test will silently skip fields with missing labels; add a separate assertion that `await input.count() > 0` for every required field to ensure none are skipped due to a labelling failure.

**Pattern 381** — WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible — Custom Focus Style Non-Text Contrast Check
```typescript
test('custom focus ring meets WCAG 1.4.11 non-text contrast (3:1)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
  const focusedEl = page.locator(':focus');
  await expect(focusedEl).toBeVisible();
  const outlineColor = await focusedEl.evaluate(el => {
    const s = getComputedStyle(el);
    return s.outlineColor;
  });
  // Parse rgb() and compute relative luminance against black background
  const match = outlineColor.match(/rgb\((\d+),\s*(\d+),\s*(\d+)\)/);
  if (match) {
    const [, r, g, b] = match.map(Number);
    const toLinear = (c: number) => {
      const s = c / 255;
      return s <= 0.04045 ? s / 12.92 : ((s + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4;
    };
    const L = 0.2126 * toLinear(r) + 0.7152 * toLinear(g) + 0.0722 * toLinear(b);
    const ratio = (L + 0.05) / (0 + 0.05); // vs black background
    expect(ratio).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(3.0);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: This test computes the focus outline colour contrast against a fixed black background — the actual contrast must be evaluated against the adjacent background colour at the focus location, which varies per page; for accurate WCAG 1.4.11 compliance, read both the `outlineColor` and the background via `getComputedStyle`, considering that `background: transparent` requires walking up the DOM tree to find the effective background colour.

**Pattern 382** — ARIA Live Region Announcement Timing with `role="status"`
```typescript
test('status live region announces async operation result', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/form');
  // Pre-render the live region so the AT has already registered it
  await expect(page.locator('[role="status"]')).toBeAttached();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
  // Wait for text to appear in the live region
  await expect(page.locator('[role="status"]')).toHaveText(/saved successfully/i, { timeout: 5000 });
  // Verify aria-live attribute is polite (not assertive for non-critical status)
  const liveValue = await page.locator('[role="status"]').getAttribute('aria-live');
  expect(['polite', null]).toContain(liveValue); // null means role implies polite
});
```
Tradeoff: Playwright captures DOM text updates but does not simulate screen reader announcement queues — a live region that updates correctly in the DOM will pass this test even if the `aria-live` container was injected after the page load (injected containers are not picked up by some AT); always pre-render `role="status"` containers in the initial HTML and only toggle their text content at runtime, never insert the container dynamically.

**Pattern 383** — WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured — Scroll Padding Validation
```typescript
test('focused element is not obscured by sticky header (WCAG 2.4.11)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/long-page');
  const interactiveEls = page.locator('a[href], button:not([disabled])');
  const count = await interactiveEls.count();
  for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(count, 20); i++) {
    await interactiveEls.nth(i).focus();
    const focused = interactiveEls.nth(i);
    const box = await focused.boundingBox();
    const headerBox = await page
      .locator('header[class*="sticky"], [data-sticky]')
      .first()
      .boundingBox();
    if (!box || !headerBox) continue;
    // The top of the focused element must be below the bottom of the sticky header
    expect(box.y).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(headerBox.y + headerBox.height);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `boundingBox()` returns coordinates in the current viewport after any browser scroll-into-view behaviour — if the browser scrolls the focused element into view but the sticky header overlaps it, the `box.y` value will still reflect the overlapped position; pair this test with a `scroll-padding-top` CSS assertion via `getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).scrollPaddingTop` to verify the root element has a padding value matching the header height.

**Pattern 384** — WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry — Verify Pre-Populated Fields in Multi-Step Form
```typescript
test('multi-step form does not ask for previously entered data (WCAG 3.3.7)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/onboarding/step-1');
  await page.getByLabel('First name').fill('Alice');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('alice@example.com');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();

  await page.waitForURL('**/step-2');
  // WCAG 3.3.7: previously provided info should be auto-populated or not re-requested
  const firstNameOnStep2 = page.getByLabel('First name');
  if (await firstNameOnStep2.count() > 0) {
    await expect(firstNameOnStep2).toHaveValue('Alice');
  }
  const emailOnStep2 = page.getByLabel('Email');
  if (await emailOnStep2.count() > 0) {
    await expect(emailOnStep2).toHaveValue('alice@example.com');
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: This test only verifies that previously entered values are retained when the same field appears again — WCAG 3.3.7 also requires that the user can confirm (rather than re-type) previously entered information, which means a read-only display of entered values with a "confirm" interaction also satisfies the criterion; update the test to accept either a pre-filled editable field or a read-only confirmation element with `aria-readonly="true"` or `disabled` attribute.

### Community Gotchas

**G276** — `autocomplete="off"` on login and checkout forms blocks browser password managers and disables WCAG 3.3.8 autocomplete support — this is a common developer workaround for "security" that actively harms accessibility
Why this matters: Developers add `autocomplete="off"` or `autocomplete="new-password"` to all inputs on login and checkout forms to prevent the browser from showing autofill UI, believing it improves security. In practice, browsers largely ignore `autocomplete="off"` for password fields per the WHATWG HTML Living Standard recommendation, so the "security benefit" is illusory. The real harm is to users: screen reader users who rely on their AT's form-fill features cannot populate fields automatically; users with motor disabilities who use switch access or eye-tracking rely on autofill to avoid repetitive precise input; users with cognitive disabilities who cannot memorise passwords depend on password managers. WCAG 3.3.8 (Level AA in WCAG 2.2) requires that re-authenticating users are not required to re-type passwords and that autocomplete is available. Setting `autocomplete="off"` directly violates this criterion for authentication fields.
Fix: Remove `autocomplete="off"` from all login inputs. Use `autocomplete="current-password"` on the password field and `autocomplete="email"` or `autocomplete="username"` on the identifier field. For new-account registration, use `autocomplete="new-password"` to allow password managers to generate and store a new credential. If a genuine security policy forbids browser autofill (e.g. for PCI-DSS CVV fields), use `autocomplete="off"` only on the CVV input and document the exemption in your accessibility conformance report.

**G277** — `role="group"` without an `aria-labelledby` or `aria-label` on a fieldset-replacement element leaves screen reader users without group context — VoiceOver announces "group" but not what the group contains
Why this matters: WCAG 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) requires that the semantic structure — including grouping of related controls — is conveyed programmatically. The HTML `<fieldset>/<legend>` pattern satisfies this natively, but developers frequently replace fieldsets with `<div role="group">` when they need full CSS control over the layout. The ARIA `group` role requires an accessible name (via `aria-labelledby` or `aria-label`) to be meaningful; without it, VoiceOver enters the group and announces "group" followed by the first control, with no indication of the group's purpose. This is especially damaging in radio button groups where the question text is a sibling `<p>` rather than a `<legend>` — screen reader users navigate to the first radio option and hear the option label but never the question. NVDA with Firefox is less affected because it reads adjacent text, but VoiceOver with Safari and JAWS with Chrome both drop the unlabelled group context.
Fix: Always provide an accessible name for `role="group"`: `<div role="group" aria-labelledby="group-heading-id">`. For radio button groups, the question `<p>` element gets an `id` and the group gets `aria-labelledby` pointing to it. Alternatively, use native `<fieldset>/<legend>` which is fully styled with modern CSS — `fieldset { border: none; padding: 0; margin: 0; }` removes the default browser border without losing semantics. Test with axe rule `group-label` which flags `role="group"` elements with no accessible name.

**G278** — `tabindex="0"` added to a `<div>` or `<span>` to make it keyboard-focusable does not grant it an interactive ARIA role — screen readers announce the element as its HTML element type with no implied action, confusing users who press Enter expecting something to happen
Why this matters: Adding `tabindex="0"` to a non-interactive element puts it in the natural tab order and allows keyboard users to focus it, but the element retains its default ARIA role (`generic` for `<div>`, `none` for `<span>`). Screen readers may announce it as blank, or announce its text content without any action hint — users pressing Enter or Space receive no response because no `keydown` handler exists for those keys, and no native click event fires. This is distinct from a `<button>` which fires `click` on both Enter and Space by default. The pattern most commonly appears in custom card components, expandable list items, and custom dropdown triggers built with `<div>` elements. It violates WCAG 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) because the role and value (state) are absent.
Fix: Replace `<div tabindex="0">` interactive patterns with the correct semantic element (`<button>` for click actions, `<a href>` for navigation, `<input type="checkbox">` for toggle state). If a `<div>` wrapper is structurally required, add both `tabindex="0"` and `role="button"` (or the appropriate ARIA role), then implement keyboard event handlers for `keydown` Enter and Space that call the same handler as the `click` event. Audit with axe rule `keyboard` which catches focusable non-interactive elements without a valid role.

**G279** — CSS `content` property text injected via `::before` or `::after` pseudo-elements is announced by some screen readers (VoiceOver, NVDA) but ignored by others (JAWS in some modes) — pseudo-element content is not a reliable vehicle for accessible text
Why this matters: Developers use CSS `::before { content: "Required — "; }` to prepend form labels with a required-field indicator or use `::after { content: " ↗"; }` to append an external-link indicator to anchor text. VoiceOver on macOS and iOS reads pseudo-element `content` strings as part of the accessible name computation; NVDA with Firefox 2024+ also reads them. However, JAWS in virtual (browse) cursor mode and certain Android TalkBack versions do not include pseudo-element text in accessible name calculations, meaning users of those AT combinations miss the required/external context entirely. The ARIA specification and HTML accessibility API mappings do not require browsers to include CSS pseudo-element content in the computed accessible name — it is browser/AT implementation-defined behaviour. Relying on it creates a compliance gap that axe-core does not flag.
Fix: Never rely solely on CSS `content` for text that conveys functional meaning (required state, link behaviour). For required indicators, use `aria-required="true"` and a visible `<span aria-hidden="true"> *</span>` inside the label. For external links, add a visually-hidden `<span class="sr-only">(opens in new tab)</span>` inside the anchor element in addition to `target="_blank" rel="noopener"`. Test by inspecting the computed accessible name with Playwright: verify that `await locator.textContent()` includes the expected text — if it only appears in CSS `content`, it will be absent from `textContent()` and AT computed name for JAWS users.

**G280** — `aria-describedby` pointing to a hidden element (`display: none` or `visibility: hidden`) silently fails — the description is not exposed to AT, leaving users without the supplementary context the developer intended
Why this matters: A common pattern is to associate an input with a hint text element using `aria-describedby="hint-id"` and then conditionally show or hide the hint with CSS. When the hint is hidden via `display: none`, browsers exclude it from the accessibility tree, and AT cannot retrieve its text as the accessible description — the `aria-describedby` reference is silently ignored. The developer believes users are receiving the hint ("Password must be 12 characters") but screen reader users never hear it. This is distinct from `aria-labelledby` pointing to a hidden element (which most browsers also ignore). The ARIA specification recommends that the referenced element be in the accessibility tree for `aria-describedby` to function — but there is no UA error, no axe-core violation, and no console warning, making this a silent failure. axe-core rule `aria-valid-attr-value` only validates that the `id` exists in the DOM, not that the referenced element is visible to AT.
Fix: Never hide `aria-describedby` targets with `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`. For conditional hints, use `aria-describedby` only when the hint element is visible, and remove or update the attribute when the hint is hidden. Alternatively, the most robust pattern is to keep hint text in the DOM with `opacity: 0; height: 0; overflow: hidden` (CSS visually-hidden) rather than `display: none` — these properties do not remove the element from the accessibility tree. Test with Playwright: `await expect(page.locator('#hint-id')).not.toHaveCSS('display', 'none')` whenever the input using `aria-describedby="hint-id"` is focused.
