## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 385** — WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance — Verify 2px Perimeter Area and 3:1 Change-of-Contrast
```typescript
test('focus indicator meets WCAG 2.4.13 area and contrast requirements', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  const button = page.getByRole('button').first();
  await button.focus();

  // Capture computed outline properties in focused state
  const focusedStyles = await button.evaluate((el) => {
    const s = window.getComputedStyle(el);
    return {
      outlineWidth: parseFloat(s.outlineWidth),
      outlineOffset: parseFloat(s.outlineOffset),
      outlineColor: s.outlineColor,
      width: el.getBoundingClientRect().width,
      height: el.getBoundingClientRect().height,
    };
  });

  // WCAG 2.4.13: outline width must be >= 2px
  expect(focusedStyles.outlineWidth).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2);

  // Verify minimum perimeter area: 4h + 4w for a rectangle
  const minArea = 4 * focusedStyles.height + 4 * focusedStyles.width;
  const actualArea = 2 * focusedStyles.outlineWidth *
    (2 * focusedStyles.width + 2 * focusedStyles.height);
  expect(actualArea).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(minArea);

  // Verify outline color is not transparent (presence check)
  expect(focusedStyles.outlineColor).not.toBe('rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)');
});
```
Tradeoff: `getComputedStyle` returns the CSS outline dimensions but cannot compute the 3:1 change-of-contrast ratio between focused and unfocused pixel states programmatically in Playwright without a pixel-diffing library; this test validates area coverage and outline presence, but a full WCAG 2.4.13 contrast assertion requires screenshot diffing with a tool like `pixelmatch` or a manual review step with the browser's colour picker against the unfocused background.

**Pattern 386** — ARIA Combobox Keyboard Contract — aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant, and Escape Behaviour
```typescript
test('combobox keyboard contract: expand, navigate, select, dismiss (WCAG 4.1.2)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');
  const combobox = page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Search' });
  await combobox.focus();

  // Listbox must be collapsed initially
  await expect(combobox).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');

  // Typing opens the popup
  await combobox.type('acc');
  await expect(combobox).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
  const listbox = page.getByRole('listbox');
  await expect(listbox).toBeVisible();

  // Arrow-down moves virtual focus via aria-activedescendant — DOM focus stays on combobox
  await combobox.press('ArrowDown');
  const activeId = await combobox.getAttribute('aria-activedescendant');
  expect(activeId).toBeTruthy();
  await expect(page.locator(`#${activeId}`)).toHaveAttribute('aria-selected', 'true');

  // Escape collapses the popup
  await combobox.press('Escape');
  await expect(combobox).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  await expect(listbox).not.toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `aria-activedescendant` keeps DOM focus on the combobox input while conveying virtual focus to AT — this is the correct ARIA APG pattern — but some older JAWS versions (pre-2022) do not announce `aria-activedescendant` changes reliably on custom listbox implementations; consider also testing with `role="option"` children explicitly carrying `id` attributes and verifying the referenced `id` exists with `page.locator('#' + activeId).count()` before asserting `aria-selected`.

**Pattern 387** — WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements — Verify Single-Pointer Alternative for Drag-to-Reorder
```typescript
test('drag-to-reorder list provides single-pointer alternative (WCAG 2.5.7)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/task-list');
  const items = page.getByRole('listitem');
  const firstItemText = await items.first().textContent();

  // Verify move-up/move-down buttons exist as non-drag alternative
  const moveUpBtn = items.first().getByRole('button', { name: /move up|reorder up/i });
  const moveDownBtn = items.first().getByRole('button', { name: /move down|reorder down/i });
  await expect(moveUpBtn.or(moveDownBtn)).toBeVisible();

  // Activate the move-down alternative and confirm reorder without dragging
  const secondItemText = await items.nth(1).textContent();
  await moveDownBtn.click();

  // After move-down, what was item 1 should now be item 2
  await expect(items.nth(1)).toHaveText(firstItemText!.trim());
  await expect(items.first()).toHaveText(secondItemText!.trim());
});
```
Tradeoff: This test validates the presence and functionality of a button-based reorder alternative but does not test the drag interaction itself — WCAG 2.5.7 requires only that a single-pointer alternative exists, not that dragging is prohibited; to catch regressions where the alternative buttons are accidentally removed, add this test to a dedicated WCAG 2.5.7 smoke suite that runs on every build, and separately test the drag interaction in a Playwright `dragTo()` test to ensure both paths remain functional.

**Pattern 388** — axe-core `resultTypes` Performance — Scan Large Pages with Violations-Only Mode
```typescript
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard page has no axe violations (optimised scan)', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // resultTypes: ['violations'] skips passes/incomplete computation — up to 8x faster
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa'])
    .options({ resultTypes: ['violations'] })
    .analyze();

  if (results.violations.length > 0) {
    await testInfo.attach('axe-violations', {
      body: JSON.stringify(results.violations, null, 2),
      contentType: 'application/json',
    });
  }
  expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
});
```
Tradeoff: `resultTypes: ['violations']` dramatically reduces scan time on content-heavy pages by omitting the computation of `passes`, `incomplete`, and `inapplicable` result arrays — the trade-off is that the resulting report cannot be used for compliance evidence (which often requires a full `passes` list) and `incomplete` items (axe's "needs review" checks) are silently dropped; reserve this optimisation for CI gate tests and run a full `resultTypes`-omitted scan nightly or pre-release to retain the complete evidence trail.

**Pattern 389** — WCAG 1.4.11 Non-Text Contrast — Icon Button Contrast Ratio Assertion via Computed Color
```typescript
test('icon buttons meet WCAG 1.4.11 non-text contrast (3:1 against background)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  const iconButtons = page.getByRole('button').filter({ has: page.locator('svg, img[role="img"]') });
  const count = await iconButtons.count();

  for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(count, 10); i++) {
    const btn = iconButtons.nth(i);
    const colors = await btn.evaluate((el) => {
      const s = window.getComputedStyle(el);
      const parentS = window.getComputedStyle(el.parentElement || document.body);
      return {
        color: s.color,          // icon fill colour (if CSS-controlled)
        background: parentS.backgroundColor,
      };
    });
    // Verify the icon colour is not identical to the background (basic presence check)
    expect(colors.color).not.toBe(colors.background);
    // Log for manual contrast verification
    console.log(`Button ${i} — icon: ${colors.color}, bg: ${colors.background}`);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `getComputedStyle` returns the CSS `color` property which controls SVG `currentColor` fills — however, SVG icons with explicit `fill` attributes or CSS `fill` overrides will not be captured by `color`; for those, inspect `fill` via `el.querySelector('svg').style.fill || getComputedStyle(el.querySelector('svg')).fill`; additionally, automated contrast ratio calculation from RGB strings requires a helper function implementing the WCAG relative luminance formula, so this pattern logs values for manual follow-up unless a utility like `@checkwcag/contrast` is added to the test suite.

**Pattern 390** — ARIA Disclosure Widget — `<details>/<summary>` vs `role="button" aria-expanded` Regression Guard
```typescript
test('disclosure widgets expose correct ARIA expanded state (WCAG 4.1.2)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/faq');

  // Test native <details>/<summary> elements
  const summaries = page.locator('details > summary');
  const nativeCount = await summaries.count();
  for (let i = 0; i < nativeCount; i++) {
    const summary = summaries.nth(i);
    const details = summary.locator('..');
    // Native details: closed by default
    await expect(details).not.toHaveAttribute('open');
    await summary.click();
    await expect(details).toHaveAttribute('open');
    await summary.click();
    await expect(details).not.toHaveAttribute('open');
  }

  // Test ARIA button-based disclosures
  const ariaToggles = page.getByRole('button', { name: /show|expand|toggle/i });
  const ariaCount = await ariaToggles.count();
  for (let i = 0; i < ariaCount; i++) {
    const toggle = ariaToggles.nth(i);
    await expect(toggle).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
    await toggle.click();
    await expect(toggle).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: Native `<details>/<summary>` elements manage expanded state via the `open` attribute automatically — no `aria-expanded` is needed or appropriate; mixing native and ARIA-based disclosures on the same page can confuse the test logic, so split these into separate test blocks; also note that Safari's VoiceOver announces `<summary>` as a disclosure triangle while NVDA/JAWS on Windows announce it as a button, so cross-AT testing is still necessary even when the automated assertion passes.

**Pattern 391** — WCAG 3.2.6 Consistent Help — Verify Help Link DOM Position is Identical Across Pages
```typescript
test('help mechanism appears in consistent DOM position across pages (WCAG 3.2.6)', async ({ page }) => {
  const pagesToCheck = ['/', '/settings', '/profile', '/billing'];
  let referenceIndex: number | null = null;

  for (const path of pagesToCheck) {
    await page.goto(path);
    await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

    // Find the help link/button in the page
    const helpLink = page.getByRole('link', { name: /help|support|contact/i }).first();
    await expect(helpLink).toBeVisible();

    // Get its position in the tab order by counting focusable predecessors
    const positionInTabOrder = await helpLink.evaluate((el) => {
      const focusable = Array.from(
        document.querySelectorAll('a[href], button:not([disabled]), [tabindex="0"]')
      );
      return focusable.indexOf(el as HTMLElement);
    });

    if (referenceIndex === null) {
      referenceIndex = positionInTabOrder;
    } else {
      // WCAG 3.2.6: help must appear in the same relative order across pages
      expect(Math.abs(positionInTabOrder - referenceIndex)).toBeLessThanOrEqual(2);
    }
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: Measuring DOM position via `focusable.indexOf` is a proxy for "same relative order" — WCAG 3.2.6 requires consistency in the visual order within the page template, not an exact tab-index number, so pages with different amounts of navigation content will shift the absolute index; using a tolerance of 2 helps here, but a more robust assertion is to verify that the help link always appears inside the same landmark region (e.g., `footer` or `[role="navigation"]`) by checking `helpLink.evaluate(el => el.closest('[role]')?.getAttribute('role'))`.

**Pattern 392** — `toMatchAriaSnapshot` — Regression Guard for Dialog Role Tree After Dynamic Open/Close
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('modal dialog aria snapshot matches expected role tree on open (Playwright 1.49+)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open settings' }).click();

  const dialog = page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Settings' });
  await expect(dialog).toBeVisible();

  // Snapshot the ARIA role tree — only roles, names, and states; no fragile text content
  await expect(dialog).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - dialog "Settings":
      - heading "Settings" [level=2]
      - group "Notifications":
        - checkbox "Email notifications"
        - checkbox "Push notifications"
      - button "Save"
      - button "Cancel"
  `);

  // After close, dialog must be removed from accessibility tree
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel' }).click();
  await expect(dialog).not.toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).toHaveCount(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `toMatchAriaSnapshot` uses a subset YAML matching syntax where listed children must appear in order but additional children are allowed by default — this means new fields added to the dialog will not fail the snapshot; if you need strict child-count enforcement, add a `count:` assertion or use `exact: true` mode introduced in Playwright 1.50, but note that `exact: true` makes the snapshot brittle when UX copy changes, so reserve strict mode for critical authentication or payment dialogs where the role tree must not drift.

**Pattern 393** — WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose — Autocomplete Token Audit Across All Form Inputs
```typescript
test('all personal data inputs carry correct autocomplete tokens (WCAG 1.3.5)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Map of label text pattern → expected autocomplete token
  const expectedTokens: Record<string, string> = {
    'first name': 'given-name',
    'last name': 'family-name',
    'email': 'email',
    'phone': 'tel',
    'address': 'street-address',
    'zip': 'postal-code',
    'city': 'address-level2',
    'country': 'country',
    'card number': 'cc-number',
    'expiry': 'cc-exp',
  };

  for (const [labelPattern, token] of Object.entries(expectedTokens)) {
    const input = page.getByLabel(new RegExp(labelPattern, 'i'));
    if (await input.count() > 0) {
      await expect(input.first()).toHaveAttribute('autocomplete', token);
    }
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `getByLabel` locates the input via its associated `<label>` element — inputs labelled only with `placeholder`, `aria-label`, or `title` will not be found by this query; supplement with `page.locator('input[name*="email"], input[type="email"]')` for inputs lacking explicit labels to avoid silent misses; also note that the `autocomplete` token list is normative in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard and WCAG 1.3.5 references it directly — verify tokens against the standard list at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-autofill.html#autofill-field when adding new fields.

**Pattern 394** — ARIA Live Region Debounce — Single Announcement for Rapid Status Updates
```typescript
test('rapid search results update produces only one live region announcement', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');

  // Capture all live region text changes during a burst of typing
  const announcements: string[] = [];
  await page.exposeFunction('captureAnnouncement', (text: string) => {
    announcements.push(text);
  });

  await page.evaluate(() => {
    const liveRegion = document.querySelector('[aria-live="polite"], [role="status"]');
    if (!liveRegion) return;
    const observer = new MutationObserver(() => {
      const text = (liveRegion as HTMLElement).textContent?.trim();
      if (text) (window as unknown as { captureAnnouncement: (t: string) => void }).captureAnnouncement(text);
    });
    observer.observe(liveRegion, { childList: true, subtree: true, characterData: true });
  });

  // Type rapidly — a debounced implementation should batch announcements
  const searchInput = page.getByRole('searchbox');
  await searchInput.type('accessibility', { delay: 50 });

  // Wait for debounce to settle (typically 300–500ms)
  await page.waitForTimeout(600);

  // A properly debounced live region should produce at most 2 announcements
  // (one for "searching..." and one for "N results found")
  expect(announcements.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(2);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.exposeFunction` with a `MutationObserver` reliably captures DOM text changes but fires synchronously on every mutation — rapidly-updating search results may still produce multiple announcements if the implementation clears and refills the live region for each keystroke; the test tolerance of `<= 2` accommodates a "searching..." interim announcement, but if the product spec guarantees a single final announcement only, tighten to `<= 1`; additionally, `page.waitForTimeout` is inherently non-deterministic across CI environments with variable CPU load — prefer `page.waitForFunction(() => window._searchComplete === true)` with a completion flag if the application exposes one.

**Pattern 395** — WCAG 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts — Verify Single-Character Shortcuts Can Be Disabled or Remapped
```typescript
test('single-character keyboard shortcuts provide a disable or remap mechanism (WCAG 2.1.4)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Check for a keyboard shortcuts settings panel
  const shortcutSettings = page.getByRole('link', { name: /keyboard shortcuts|accessibility settings/i })
    .or(page.getByRole('button', { name: /keyboard shortcuts/i }));

  const hasShortcutSettings = await shortcutSettings.count() > 0;

  if (!hasShortcutSettings) {
    // If no settings UI, verify single-key shortcuts only activate when focus is on a widget
    // Press 'j' (common single-key shortcut) while focused on the document body
    await page.locator('body').focus();
    await page.keyboard.press('j');
    // No navigation or action should have occurred — verify URL unchanged
    const urlBefore = page.url();
    await page.keyboard.press('j');
    expect(page.url()).toBe(urlBefore);
  } else {
    // Settings UI exists — verify it contains a toggle for shortcuts
    await shortcutSettings.first().click();
    const disableToggle = page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: /disable.*shortcuts|turn off.*shortcuts/i })
      .or(page.getByRole('switch', { name: /shortcuts/i }));
    await expect(disableToggle).toBeVisible();
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: This test covers the two most common WCAG 2.1.4 compliance paths — a dedicated settings UI and focus-scoped activation — but the standard also allows a third path: key remapping; if your application uses a library like `hotkeys-js` or `mousetrap`, verify in the library's configuration that shortcuts are scoped to `INPUT`, `TEXTAREA`, and `SELECT` elements by default (most libraries do this), which satisfies the "only when focused" exception without requiring a settings panel; document the chosen compliance path in your accessibility conformance report to prevent future developers from accidentally adding unfocused global shortcuts.

**Pattern 396** — Playwright Forced Colors (Windows High Contrast) — Verify Layout Integrity Under `forced-colors: active`
```typescript
test('application remains usable under forced-colors: active (Windows High Contrast)', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    colorScheme: 'dark',
    forcedColors: 'active',
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/');

  // Key interactive elements must remain visible under forced colors
  const primaryButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: /submit|continue|save/i }).first();
  await expect(primaryButton).toBeVisible();

  // Check that custom focus rings are not hidden by forced-colors override
  await primaryButton.focus();
  const outlineStyle = await primaryButton.evaluate((el) =>
    window.getComputedStyle(el).outlineStyle
  );
  expect(outlineStyle).not.toBe('none');

  // Verify text inputs remain visible
  const inputs = page.getByRole('textbox');
  if (await inputs.count() > 0) {
    await expect(inputs.first()).toBeVisible();
  }

  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: Playwright's `forcedColors: 'active'` emulates the `forced-colors` CSS media query which browsers use in Windows High Contrast mode — this accurately reflects how the browser renders the page, but it does not simulate the OS-level forced-colour palette replacement that happens in actual High Contrast mode; real testing requires a Windows machine with High Contrast Mode enabled and manual AT testing, because Windows overrides browser CSS variables and custom properties at the OS level in ways the emulation cannot replicate; treat this test as a regression guard for CSS `forced-colors` media query compliance, not as a substitute for manual High Contrast testing.

**Pattern 397** — WCAG 1.3.1 Table Semantics — Verify `scope`, `headers`, and `aria-sort` on Data Tables
```typescript
test('data table has correct scope attributes and aria-sort on sortable columns (WCAG 1.3.1)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports');

  const table = page.getByRole('table').first();
  await expect(table).toBeVisible();

  // All column headers must have scope="col"
  const colHeaders = table.locator('th:not([scope="row"])');
  const colCount = await colHeaders.count();
  for (let i = 0; i < colCount; i++) {
    await expect(colHeaders.nth(i)).toHaveAttribute('scope', 'col');
  }

  // Sortable headers must carry aria-sort
  const sortableHeaders = table.locator('th[data-sortable], th[role="columnheader"]');
  const sortableCount = await sortableHeaders.count();
  for (let i = 0; i < sortableCount; i++) {
    const ariaSort = await sortableHeaders.nth(i).getAttribute('aria-sort');
    expect(['ascending', 'descending', 'none', 'other']).toContain(ariaSort);
  }

  // Click a sortable header and verify aria-sort updates
  if (sortableCount > 0) {
    await sortableHeaders.first().click();
    const updatedSort = await sortableHeaders.first().getAttribute('aria-sort');
    expect(['ascending', 'descending']).toContain(updatedSort);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `scope="col"` on `<th>` elements is sufficient for simple tables without row groups — for complex tables with merged cells or row headers, `headers` attribute referencing the correct `<th id>` values is required and `scope` alone will cause screen reader announcement errors; axe-core's `td-headers-attr` and `th-has-data-cells` rules catch most of these cases automatically, so run axe alongside this structural test rather than relying solely on the manual scope assertion.

**Pattern 398** — ARIA Treeview Keyboard Contract — Arrow Key Navigation and `aria-expanded` State
```typescript
test('treeview supports arrow-key navigation and reports aria-expanded correctly (WCAG 4.1.2)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/file-explorer');

  const tree = page.getByRole('tree');
  const rootItems = tree.getByRole('treeitem', { level: 1 });
  await rootItems.first().focus();

  // Right arrow expands a collapsed node
  await expect(rootItems.first()).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowRight');
  await expect(rootItems.first()).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');

  // Right arrow on an expanded node moves focus to first child
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowRight');
  const firstChild = tree.getByRole('treeitem', { level: 2 }).first();
  await expect(firstChild).toBeFocused();

  // Left arrow on a child node moves focus back to parent
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowLeft');
  await expect(rootItems.first()).toBeFocused();

  // Left arrow on an expanded parent collapses it
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowLeft');
  await expect(rootItems.first()).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');

  // Down arrow moves to next visible item
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowDown');
  await expect(rootItems.nth(1)).toBeFocused();
});
```
Tradeoff: The ARIA APG treeview pattern requires `aria-level`, `aria-setsize`, and `aria-posinset` on each `treeitem` for screen readers to announce position context (e.g., "Item 2 of 5, level 3") — this test does not validate those attributes; add a separate assertion `expect(await firstChild.getAttribute('aria-level')).toBe('2')` to catch trees that implement navigation correctly but omit position metadata; also note that `getByRole('treeitem', { level: N })` filtering by level is a Playwright convenience that relies on `aria-level` being set, so the test will silently find no children if the implementation omits `aria-level`.

**Pattern 399** — WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification — Validate `aria-invalid` and Linked Error Message on Blur
```typescript
test('form input sets aria-invalid and links error message on invalid blur (WCAG 3.3.1)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/register');

  const emailInput = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /email/i });
  await emailInput.fill('not-an-email');
  await emailInput.blur();

  // WCAG 3.3.1: invalid state must be programmatically exposed
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');

  // Error message must be associated via aria-describedby or aria-errormessage
  const describedBy = await emailInput.getAttribute('aria-describedby');
  const errorMessage = await emailInput.getAttribute('aria-errormessage');
  expect(describedBy || errorMessage).toBeTruthy();

  // The referenced error element must be visible and contain meaningful text
  const errorId = errorMessage || describedBy;
  const errorEl = page.locator(`#${errorId?.split(' ')[0]}`);
  await expect(errorEl).toBeVisible();
  const errorText = await errorEl.textContent();
  expect(errorText?.trim().length).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  // Playwright 1.50+: toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage assertion
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/.+/);
});
```
Tradeoff: `aria-errormessage` is semantically more precise than `aria-describedby` for error messages because it explicitly signals error content to AT — however, `aria-errormessage` requires the referenced element to be visible (not `display: none`) and `aria-invalid` must be `true` simultaneously for AT to announce it; `aria-describedby` has broader AT support but mixes error text with hint text; Playwright's `toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` (v1.50+) validates the `aria-errormessage` reference chain including visibility — use it as the primary assertion and fall back to `aria-describedby` inspection only for legacy codebases that predate `aria-errormessage` support.

### Community Gotchas

**G281** — `role="presentation"` or `role="none"` applied to a focusable element (`<a href>`, `<button>`, `<input>`) does not remove it from the accessibility tree — browsers ignore the role override on interactive elements and most AT still announces them with their native role
Why this matters: Developers use `role="none"` or `role="presentation"` on decorative wrapper elements to remove them from the accessibility tree, which is correct. However, they sometimes apply these roles to the interactive elements themselves to "hide" them from AT while keeping them visually clickable — for example, `<button role="presentation">X</button>` on a close button that "shouldn't be announced". The ARIA specification explicitly states that `role="none"` is ignored (has no effect) when applied to a focusable element; browsers map the element to its native role regardless. The result is that the button is still announced as "button" but with no accessible name (since the developer likely also removed the label when trying to hide it), creating a confusing unnamed interactive element. axe-core rule `presentation-role-conflict` flags this pattern at the violation level.
Fix: Never apply `role="none"` to interactive elements. To make a button decorative, use `aria-hidden="true"` only when the button is genuinely redundant (e.g., a duplicate click target where a labelled sibling button exists). To hide a close button from AT when it is the only dismiss mechanism, instead give it an accessible name with `aria-label="Close dialog"`. To remove a wrapper `<div>` from the tree, `role="none"` is appropriate and correct — apply it only to non-focusable container elements.

**G282** — CSS `pointer-events: none` removes mouse interactability but does not remove keyboard focus or ARIA role — keyboard users can still tab to and activate visually-disabled elements that only have `pointer-events: none`
Why this matters: Designers use `pointer-events: none; opacity: 0.4;` as a visual "disabled" state for buttons or links that are conditionally unavailable. This prevents mouse clicks, so manual testers often pass the element as "correctly disabled". However, keyboard users can still Tab to the element, receive focus, and press Enter/Space to activate it — because `pointer-events` only suppresses pointer device events, not keyboard events or the element's ARIA role. The element has no `disabled` attribute, so AT announces it as an enabled control (no "dimmed" or "grayed" announcement). Activating it can trigger the underlying action handler if the JavaScript `click` handler doesn't also check the disabled state. This is a WCAG 4.1.2 violation (role and state mismatch) and a WCAG 2.1.1 violation (keyboard path bypasses intended restriction).
Fix: Use the HTML `disabled` attribute for `<button>` and `<input>` elements — this removes them from the tab order, prevents activation, and causes AT to announce them as "dimmed" or "unavailable". For elements that must remain focusable but not activatable (e.g., a button in a loading state), use `aria-disabled="true"` plus a `keydown` handler that calls `event.preventDefault()` for Enter/Space, and set `tabindex="0"` explicitly. Never use `pointer-events: none` alone as an accessibility-complete disabled state.

**G283** — `aria-label` on a `<div role="group">` or `<fieldset>` does not override the accessible name computed from child text in all AT combinations — `aria-labelledby` pointing to a visible heading element has broader AT support for group names
Why this matters: When a developer groups related controls inside a `<div role="group" aria-label="Shipping address">`, JAWS 2023+ and NVDA compute the group's accessible name correctly from `aria-label`. However, VoiceOver on iOS (prior to iOS 17) ignores `aria-label` on `role="group"` elements that contain focusable children with their own text, instead computing the name from the concatenation of child text — resulting in an overly verbose or garbled group announcement. Using `aria-labelledby` pointing to a visible `<h3 id="shipping-heading">Shipping address</h3>` element has consistent support across all major AT and browser combinations because it references existing DOM text rather than an attribute-injected string, which aligns with how browsers compute accessible names per the ARIA in HTML specification.
Fix: Prefer `aria-labelledby` over `aria-label` for group/fieldset labelling when a visible label element already exists in the DOM. Structure the markup as `<div role="group" aria-labelledby="shipping-heading"><h3 id="shipping-heading">Shipping address</h3>...</div>`. If no visible heading exists, use a visually-hidden `<span id="group-label" class="sr-only">Group purpose</span>` and reference it via `aria-labelledby` — this is more robustly supported than `aria-label` on group containers across the AT combinations in the current testing matrix.

**G284** — `window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` JavaScript checks and CSS `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` only suppress animations when the OS accessibility setting is active — Playwright's `reducedMotion: 'reduce'` emulation flag must be set at browser context creation, not page load, to reliably emulate this preference in tests
Why this matters: Developers write WCAG 2.3.3 animation-from-interaction tests using `page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' })` called after `page.goto()`. In Playwright, `emulateMedia` called post-navigation does correctly update the media query value, but CSS transitions and JavaScript animation setup code that runs during page initialisation (`DOMContentLoaded`, React `useEffect`) have already evaluated `prefers-reduced-motion` and may have already set up `IntersectionObserver`-triggered animations based on the non-reduced value. The animations fire on first scroll before the test's emulation takes effect, causing false passes. Setting `reducedMotion: 'reduce'` in `browser.newContext({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' })` applies the preference before any navigation, ensuring all initialisation code reads the reduced preference.
Fix: Always set motion preferences at context creation: `const context = await browser.newContext({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' })`. If using Playwright fixtures, configure `use: { reducedMotion: 'reduce' }` in `playwright.config.ts` for the relevant project block. For tests that need to compare both states (reduced vs normal), create two separate browser contexts rather than toggling `emulateMedia` mid-test. Also verify CSS transition-duration is `0ms` or `1ms` under the media query by asserting `await page.locator('.animated').evaluate(el => getComputedStyle(el).transitionDuration)` returns a near-zero value.

**G285** — `aria-hidden="true"` on a `<svg>` icon inside an `<a>` or `<button>` is correct — but omitting `aria-hidden` on the `<svg>` and relying on the browser to ignore SVG content in accessible name computation is unreliable across AT combinations
Why this matters: An icon-only button pattern like `<button><svg>...</svg><span class="sr-only">Close</span></button>` works correctly when `aria-hidden="true"` is absent from the `<svg>` — most browsers exclude decorative inline SVG from accessible name computation automatically. However, if the `<svg>` contains a `<title>` child element (added by icon authoring tools like Figma export or SVGO), browsers include the `<title>` text in the accessible name computation. The button may then be announced as "remove Close" or "x Close" (title text + sr-only text concatenated) instead of just "Close". JAWS with Chrome has exhibited this behaviour with SVGs containing `<title>File icon</title>`, and axe-core rule `button-name` will pass because a name is present — but the announced name is garbled. This defect is invisible to automated tools and easy to miss in manual testing if testers only listen for the presence of a name rather than its quality.
Fix: Always add `aria-hidden="true"` and `focusable="false"` to decorative inline SVGs inside interactive elements: `<svg aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">`. Remove `<title>` elements from decorative SVGs at build time using an SVGO plugin (`removeTitle: true`). Verify the final accessible name with `await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Close' })).toBeVisible()` — Playwright's `getByRole` with `name:` only matches when the computed accessible name exactly equals the expected string, catching concatenation artifacts that axe-core misses.

## Cycle 62 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 400** — WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) — Verify Focused Component Partially Visible Under Sticky Header
```typescript
test('focused element not completely hidden under sticky header (WCAG 2.4.11)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/long-form-page');

  // Get sticky header height to use as obscuration threshold
  const header = page.locator('header[data-sticky], .sticky-header, [style*="position: sticky"]').first();
  const headerBox = await header.boundingBox();
  const headerBottom = headerBox ? headerBox.y + headerBox.height : 0;

  // Tab through focusable elements and verify none are completely obscured
  const focusableCount = await page.locator('a, button, input, select, textarea, [tabindex="0"]').count();
  for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(focusableCount, 20); i++) {
    await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
    const focused = page.locator(':focus');
    const focusedBox = await focused.boundingBox();

    if (focusedBox) {
      // WCAG 2.4.11: focused element must NOT be completely hidden
      // i.e., at least some part of it must be below the sticky header
      const elementBottom = focusedBox.y + focusedBox.height;
      expect(elementBottom).toBeGreaterThan(headerBottom);
    }
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: This test validates WCAG 2.4.11 (AA — partial visibility sufficient) rather than 2.4.12 (AAA — full visibility required) — it passes when any pixel of the focused component is visible below the sticky header, so a component where only 1px is visible will incorrectly pass; for stricter coverage add `expect(focusedBox.y).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(headerBottom)` to require the top edge of the focused element to be at or below the header bottom, effectively testing the AAA criterion; also note that `css scroll-padding-top` is the canonical fix for this defect and its effective value can be asserted via `page.locator('html').evaluate(el => getComputedStyle(el).scrollPaddingTop)`.

**Pattern 401** — WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — Assert 24×24 CSS Pixel Minimum on All Interactive Controls
```typescript
test('interactive controls meet 24×24 CSS pixel target size minimum (WCAG 2.5.8)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Collect all interactive elements excluding inline text links (SC 2.5.8 exception)
  const targets = page.locator('button, [role="button"], input[type="checkbox"], input[type="radio"], select, [role="menuitem"], [role="tab"], [role="switch"]');
  const count = await targets.count();

  const failures: string[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const el = targets.nth(i);
    const box = await el.boundingBox();
    if (!box) continue;

    const label = await el.getAttribute('aria-label') ?? await el.textContent() ?? `element[${i}]`;

    // WCAG 2.5.8: minimum 24×24 CSS pixels
    if (box.width < 24 || box.height < 24) {
      failures.push(`"${label.trim()}" is ${Math.round(box.width)}×${Math.round(box.height)}px (min 24×24)`);
    }
  }

  expect(failures, `Target size violations:\n${failures.join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: This test applies the strict 24×24 pixel floor without evaluating the spacing-offset exception defined in SC 2.5.8 — a 20×20 button with 4px gaps to all neighbours is technically compliant but will fail this test; to implement the spacing exception, compute each element's bounding box centroid, draw a 24px-diameter circle, and assert it does not intersect neighbouring elements' circles using `Math.hypot(cx1 - cx2, cy1 - cy2) >= 24`; also, `boundingBox()` returns the CSS layout box including padding but excluding CSS `transform: scale()` visual enlargement, so visually scaled-up small buttons may still fail — verify using `getComputedStyle` for `transform` values.

**Pattern 402** — WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry — Verify Multi-Step Form Auto-Populates Previously Entered Data
```typescript
test('checkout form auto-populates billing address from shipping (WCAG 3.3.7)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/shipping');

  // Step 1: fill shipping address
  await page.getByLabel(/first name/i).fill('Jane');
  await page.getByLabel(/last name/i).fill('Smith');
  await page.getByLabel(/street address/i).fill('123 Main St');
  await page.getByLabel(/city/i).fill('Springfield');
  await page.getByLabel(/zip/i).fill('12345');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /continue/i }).click();

  // Step 2: billing — use "same as shipping" checkbox
  await page.waitForURL('**/checkout/billing');
  const sameAsShipping = page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: /same as shipping/i });
  await expect(sameAsShipping).toBeVisible();
  await sameAsShipping.check();

  // WCAG 3.3.7: previously entered data must auto-populate
  await expect(page.getByLabel(/first name/i)).toHaveValue('Jane');
  await expect(page.getByLabel(/last name/i)).toHaveValue('Smith');
  await expect(page.getByLabel(/street address/i)).toHaveValue('123 Main St');
  await expect(page.getByLabel(/city/i)).toHaveValue('Springfield');
  await expect(page.getByLabel(/zip/i)).toHaveValue('12345');
});
```
Tradeoff: This test validates the "same as shipping" auto-populate path — the most common WCAG 3.3.7 implementation — but does not test the alternative compliant path where the billing step shows previously entered values as selectable options rather than auto-filling; for full coverage, also test a flow where the user selects from saved addresses and verify no re-entry of complete address data is required; the criterion does not require auto-populate specifically (selectable options satisfy it), so a design that shows a dropdown of prior entries would pass WCAG 3.3.7 even if `toHaveValue` assertions here would fail.

**Pattern 403** — WCAG 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication — Assert Password Field Allows Paste and Browser Autofill
```typescript
test('login form allows paste and autofill in password field (WCAG 3.3.8)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');

  const passwordInput = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /password/i })
    .or(page.locator('input[type="password"]'));

  // WCAG 3.3.8: paste must not be blocked
  await passwordInput.click();
  // Simulate clipboard paste via programmatic value injection
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    const input = document.querySelector('input[type="password"]') as HTMLInputElement;
    const nativeInputValueSetter = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(window.HTMLInputElement.prototype, 'value')?.set;
    nativeInputValueSetter?.call(input, 'PastedPassword123!');
    input.dispatchEvent(new Event('input', { bubbles: true }));
  });

  // Field must not clear itself, prevent input, or throw after paste simulation
  const value = await passwordInput.inputValue();
  expect(value.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  // Autocomplete attribute must not be 'off' — disabling autocomplete blocks password managers
  const autocomplete = await passwordInput.getAttribute('autocomplete');
  expect(autocomplete).not.toBe('off');

  // Acceptable values: 'current-password', 'new-password', or null (browser default)
  if (autocomplete !== null) {
    expect(['current-password', 'new-password']).toContain(autocomplete);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: Playwright's `page.evaluate` paste simulation bypasses the browser clipboard API and `paste` event — it cannot detect JavaScript `paste` event listeners that call `event.preventDefault()` to block paste at the DOM event level; to catch event-listener-based paste blocking, use `page.keyboard.press('Control+V')` after writing to the clipboard via `page.context().grantPermissions(['clipboard-read', 'clipboard-write'])` and `page.evaluate(() => navigator.clipboard.writeText('test'))`, then assert the field's `inputValue()` equals `'test'`; additionally, `autocomplete="new-password"` is correct on registration forms but `autocomplete="current-password"` is required on login forms for password managers to fill credentials — using the wrong token causes password managers to not offer autofill, which is a WCAG 3.3.8 barrier even though axe-core does not currently flag this.

**Pattern 404** — WCAG 1.4.13 Content on Hover — Validate Tooltip Dismissable, Hoverable, and Persistent
```typescript
test('tooltip dismissable, hoverable, and persistent on trigger hover (WCAG 1.4.13)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/components/tooltip-demo');

  const trigger = page.getByRole('button', { name: /info/i }).first();

  // Hover trigger to show tooltip
  await trigger.hover();
  const tooltip = page.getByRole('tooltip').first();
  await expect(tooltip).toBeVisible();

  // 1. Hoverable: moving mouse over tooltip must keep it visible
  await tooltip.hover();
  await expect(tooltip).toBeVisible();

  // 2. Persistent: tooltip must stay visible without user action
  await page.waitForTimeout(3000);
  await expect(tooltip).toBeVisible();

  // 3. Dismissable: Escape key must dismiss without moving focus
  await trigger.hover();
  await expect(tooltip).toBeVisible();
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(tooltip).toBeHidden();

  // Focus must not have moved on Escape dismiss
  await expect(trigger).toBeFocused();
});
```
Tradeoff: WCAG 1.4.13 applies to author-created hover content — CSS-only tooltips using `:hover` pseudo-class satisfy "persistent" and "hoverable" by nature but cannot be dismissed with Escape since there is no JavaScript handler; pure CSS tooltips technically fail the "dismissable" requirement unless a CSS-only Escape-key dismiss mechanism exists (which is not possible in pure CSS); this test requires a JavaScript-managed tooltip; also, the 3-second persistence check (`waitForTimeout(3000)`) will cause the test to be slow — consider instead verifying the tooltip has no CSS `animation-duration` or auto-hide timer by inspecting computed styles or component props rather than waiting.

**Pattern 405** — WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order — Validate Modal Dialog Traps Focus and Returns Focus on Close
```typescript
test('modal dialog traps focus and returns focus to trigger on close (WCAG 2.4.3)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/components/modal-demo');

  const openButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: /open modal/i });
  await openButton.click();

  const dialog = page.getByRole('dialog');
  await expect(dialog).toBeVisible();

  // Focus must be inside dialog on open
  const focusedEl = page.locator(':focus');
  await expect(dialog).toContainText(await focusedEl.textContent() ?? '');

  // Tab through all focusable elements — focus must not leave dialog
  const focusableInDialog = await dialog.locator('a, button, input, select, textarea, [tabindex="0"]').count();
  for (let i = 0; i < focusableInDialog + 2; i++) {
    await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
    const currentFocus = await page.evaluate(() => document.activeElement?.closest('[role="dialog"]') !== null);
    expect(currentFocus).toBe(true);
  }

  // Close dialog and verify focus returns to trigger
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(dialog).toBeHidden();
  await expect(openButton).toBeFocused();
});
```
Tradeoff: The focus-containment loop uses `document.activeElement?.closest('[role="dialog"]')` which works for dialogs where the role is on a direct ancestor — it fails for nested dialogs or dialogs implemented with a `<dialog>` element whose `role` is implicitly "dialog" but whose markup hierarchy differs; use `page.locator('dialog, [role="dialog"]').first().locator(':focus')` for more robust containment checking; also note that `aria-modal="true"` on the dialog element is supposed to instruct AT to treat content outside the dialog as inert, but VoiceOver on macOS prior to Ventura ignores `aria-modal` — the only reliable cross-AT focus trap is programmatic `inert` attribute on all sibling/ancestor nodes outside the dialog, which should also be tested by asserting `await page.locator('main').getAttribute('inert')` is not null when the dialog is open.

**Pattern 406** — WCAG 1.3.4 Orientation — Verify Layout Does Not Lock to Portrait or Landscape
```typescript
test('page renders without data loss in both portrait and landscape orientations (WCAG 1.3.4)', async ({ browser }) => {
  // Portrait viewport
  const portraitContext = await browser.newContext({ viewport: { width: 390, height: 844 } });
  const portraitPage = await portraitContext.newPage();
  await portraitPage.goto('/checkout');

  // All critical form fields must be visible and accessible in portrait
  await expect(portraitPage.getByLabel(/card number/i)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(portraitPage.getByLabel(/expiry/i)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(portraitPage.getByRole('button', { name: /pay/i })).toBeVisible();
  await portraitContext.close();

  // Landscape viewport (same device, rotated)
  const landscapeContext = await browser.newContext({ viewport: { width: 844, height: 390 } });
  const landscapePage = await landscapeContext.newPage();
  await landscapePage.goto('/checkout');

  // Same controls must be accessible in landscape — no forced scroll lock message
  await expect(landscapePage.getByLabel(/card number/i)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(landscapePage.getByLabel(/expiry/i)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(landscapePage.getByRole('button', { name: /pay/i })).toBeVisible();

  // No "rotate your device" overlay should be present
  await expect(landscapePage.getByText(/rotate your device/i)).toHaveCount(0);
  await landscapeContext.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: Testing at specific iPhone 12 Pro dimensions (390×844) is device-specific — WCAG 1.3.4 requires content to not be restricted to a single display orientation without essential reason, so the test should be read as a proxy for "no CSS `@media (orientation)` with `display: none` or `pointer-events: none` on critical content" rather than a pixel-perfect responsive test; additionally, this test uses two separate `browser.newContext()` calls which is slower than `page.setViewportSize()` but more accurately represents orientation change since Playwright cannot rotate an existing viewport; for a complete test, also check that JavaScript `screen.orientation.lock()` is not called unconditionally (check for it in source or via `page.evaluate(() => screen.orientation)` state assertions).

**Pattern 407** — WCAG 1.4.12 Text Spacing — Verify No Content Loss When Spacing Overrides Applied
```typescript
test('no content loss or overflow when WCAG 1.4.12 text spacing overrides applied', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/article');

  // Inject the WCAG 1.4.12 spacing bookmarklet CSS overrides
  await page.addStyleTag({
    content: `
      * {
        line-height: 1.5 !important;
        letter-spacing: 0.12em !important;
        word-spacing: 0.16em !important;
      }
      p {
        margin-bottom: 2em !important;
      }
    `
  });

  // Wait for reflow
  await page.waitForTimeout(300);

  // Verify no text is clipped (scrollWidth must not exceed clientWidth for key containers)
  const overflowViolations = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const containers = document.querySelectorAll('p, h1, h2, h3, nav, main, article, section');
    const violations: string[] = [];
    containers.forEach(el => {
      if (el.scrollWidth > el.clientWidth + 2) {
        violations.push(`<${el.tagName.toLowerCase()}> scrollWidth(${el.scrollWidth}) > clientWidth(${el.clientWidth})`);
      }
    });
    return violations;
  });

  expect(overflowViolations, `Text spacing overflow violations:\n${overflowViolations.join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);

  // Critical interactive elements must still be operable after reflow
  await expect(page.getByRole('button').first()).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: The `scrollWidth > clientWidth + 2` heuristic catches horizontal text overflow clipping — but it misses vertical overflow clipping where a fixed-height container clips overflowing text vertically; extend the check to `el.scrollHeight > el.clientHeight + 2` on elements with `overflow: hidden` in computed styles, which can be obtained via `getComputedStyle(el).overflow`; also, injecting `!important` overrides with `addStyleTag` does not perfectly replicate the WCAG 1.4.12 test methodology described in the Understanding document (which uses a browser bookmarklet), because author `!important` rules in the existing stylesheet may still win over injected `!important` when specificity is equal and the injected stylesheet is inserted last — verify with `getComputedStyle` rather than trusting the injection.

**Pattern 408** — WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name — Verify Accessible Name Contains Visible Button Label Text
```typescript
test('button accessible names contain visible label text (WCAG 2.5.3)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/product-listing');

  const buttons = page.getByRole('button');
  const count = await buttons.count();

  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const btn = buttons.nth(i);
    const visibleText = (await btn.textContent())?.trim().toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, ' ') ?? '';
    if (!visibleText) continue; // Skip icon-only buttons with no visible text

    const accessibleName = (await btn.getAttribute('aria-label') ?? '').toLowerCase().trim();

    if (accessibleName) {
      // WCAG 2.5.3: aria-label must BEGIN WITH or CONTAIN the visible text
      expect(
        accessibleName.includes(visibleText),
        `Button visible text "${visibleText}" not found in aria-label "${accessibleName}"`
      ).toBe(true);
    }
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: WCAG 2.5.3 requires that the accessible name begins with or contains the visible label text — this test checks containment which is slightly more permissive than the "starts with" intent of the criterion; the specification's intent is that voice control users can say the visible label to activate the control — so `aria-label="Delete item from cart"` on a button labelled "Delete" passes because "delete" is contained in the name, but `aria-label="Remove from cart"` on a button labelled "Delete" fails because "delete" is not in the accessible name; note that `btn.textContent()` includes text from all descendant nodes including screen-reader-only `<span class="sr-only">` content, so if a button has `<span class="sr-only">selected</span> Add to cart`, the visible text is "Add to cart" but `textContent()` returns "selected Add to cart" — use `btn.innerText()` via `btn.evaluate(el => el.innerText)` to get only visible text.

**Pattern 409** — WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages — Validate `aria-live` Region Announces Search Result Count Without Focus Move
```typescript
test('search result count announced via aria-live without focus movement (WCAG 4.1.3)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');

  // Track live region announcements
  const announcements: string[] = [];
  await page.exposeFunction('recordAnnouncement', (text: string) => {
    announcements.push(text);
  });

  await page.evaluate(() => {
    const observer = new MutationObserver((mutations) => {
      mutations.forEach(m => {
        m.addedNodes.forEach(node => {
          if (node.textContent?.trim()) {
            (window as any).recordAnnouncement(node.textContent.trim());
          }
        });
      });
    });
    document.querySelectorAll('[aria-live]').forEach(el => {
      observer.observe(el, { childList: true, subtree: true, characterData: true });
    });
  });

  const searchInput = page.getByRole('searchbox');
  await searchInput.fill('accessibility');
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');

  // Wait for results
  await page.waitForSelector('[data-testid="results-list"]');

  // WCAG 4.1.3: status message announced without focus move
  await expect(searchInput).toBeFocused();
  expect(announcements.some(a => /\d+\s+results?/i.test(a))).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: The `MutationObserver` approach only captures text that is dynamically inserted into the live region as new child nodes — it misses announcements made by changing the `textContent` directly via `el.textContent = '...'` (a `characterData` mutation, not a `childList` mutation) or via `el.innerText`; add `characterData: true` to `MutationObserver` options and handle `characterData` mutations in the callback to capture direct text node updates; also, `aria-live="assertive"` regions announce immediately and interrupt current AT speech — verify the search results region uses `aria-live="polite"` (not assertive) since result counts are non-urgent status messages and `assertive` would violate WCAG best practice by interrupting in-progress screen reader announcements.

**Pattern 410** — WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color — Verify Required Field Indicators Use More Than Color Alone
```typescript
test('required form fields not indicated by color alone (WCAG 1.4.1)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/registration');

  const requiredInputs = page.locator('input[required], [aria-required="true"]');
  const count = await requiredInputs.count();

  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const input = requiredInputs.nth(i);
    const label = page.locator(`label[for="${await input.getAttribute('id')}"]`);

    if (await label.count() === 0) continue;

    const labelText = await label.textContent() ?? '';

    // WCAG 1.4.1: required indication must not rely on color alone
    // Check for non-color indicators: asterisk, "(required)" text, or aria-required
    const hasAsterisk = labelText.includes('*');
    const hasRequiredText = /required/i.test(labelText);
    const hasAriaRequired = await input.getAttribute('aria-required') === 'true';
    const hasHtmlRequired = await input.getAttribute('required') !== null;

    expect(
      hasAsterisk || hasRequiredText || hasAriaRequired || hasHtmlRequired,
      `Required field "${labelText.trim()}" has no non-color indicator`
    ).toBe(true);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: This test validates the presence of a non-color indicator but does not validate that the indicator is visually perceivable or that its meaning is explained — WCAG 1.4.1 best practice requires that if asterisks are used to indicate required fields, a legend explaining the convention (e.g., "* Required field") appears near the form; to test for the legend, assert `await page.getByText(/\* required/i).or(page.getByText(/asterisk.*required/i)).count()` is greater than zero on forms that use asterisk notation; also, this test uses `input[required]` which is the HTML attribute, but some frameworks remove the `required` attribute and use only `aria-required="true"` for custom validation — ensure both are checked as the test already does.

**Pattern 411** — WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard — Validate Custom Drag-and-Drop Widget Has Keyboard Alternative (WCAG 2.5.7)
```typescript
test('drag-and-drop list has keyboard reorder alternative (WCAG 2.1.1 / WCAG 2.5.7)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/task-board');

  const draggableItems = page.locator('[draggable="true"], [role="option"], [data-rbd-draggable-id]');
  const firstItem = draggableItems.first();

  // Focus the first draggable item
  await firstItem.focus();

  // Keyboard alternative must be operable — Space to pick up
  await page.keyboard.press('Space');
  const isGrabbed = await firstItem.getAttribute('aria-grabbed');
  expect(isGrabbed).toBe('true');

  // Arrow keys must move the item
  await page.keyboard.press('ArrowDown');
  const secondItem = draggableItems.nth(1);
  const afterMoveText = await secondItem.textContent();

  // Confirm item moved by pressing Space to drop
  await page.keyboard.press('Space');
  const firstItemAfterDrop = draggableItems.first();
  const firstItemText = await firstItemAfterDrop.textContent();

  // Original second item should now be first
  expect(firstItemText).toBe(afterMoveText);
});
```
Tradeoff: The `aria-grabbed` attribute was deprecated in ARIA 1.1 and removed in ARIA 1.2 — modern accessible drag-and-drop implementations use `aria-pressed` (for pick-up mode toggle buttons) or custom `aria-describedby` instructions instead; if the application uses a modern implementation without `aria-grabbed`, this assertion will fail with a false negative; check for `aria-describedby` on the draggable item pointing to instructions like "Press Space to pick up, arrow keys to move, Space to drop" and assert that text is present; also, `react-beautiful-dnd` (commonly used) does implement this keyboard pattern but uses `data-rbd-*` attributes — the locator `[data-rbd-draggable-id]` handles this library's elements correctly.

**Pattern 412** — WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose — Verify autocomplete Token Correctness on Common Personal Data Fields
```typescript
test('personal data input fields have correct HTML autocomplete tokens (WCAG 1.3.5)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/profile/edit');

  const autocompleteMap: Record<string, string> = {
    'given-name': 'given-name',
    'family-name': 'family-name',
    'email': 'email',
    'tel': 'tel',
    'street-address': 'street-address',
    'postal-code': 'postal-code',
    'country': 'country',
    'bday': 'bday',
    'organization': 'organization',
  };

  for (const [token, expectedValue] of Object.entries(autocompleteMap)) {
    const input = page.locator(`input[autocomplete="${token}"], input[autocomplete*="${token}"]`).first();
    if (await input.count() === 0) continue; // Field may not exist on this page

    const actualAutocomplete = await input.getAttribute('autocomplete');
    // WCAG 1.3.5: autocomplete value must be a valid WHATWG token
    expect(
      actualAutocomplete,
      `Input with expected token "${token}" has incorrect autocomplete: "${actualAutocomplete}"`
    ).toContain(expectedValue);

    // type must not conflict with autocomplete token
    const inputType = await input.getAttribute('type') ?? 'text';
    if (token === 'email') expect(inputType).toBe('email');
    if (token === 'tel') expect(['tel', 'text']).toContain(inputType);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: The autocomplete token map above covers common personal data fields, but WCAG 1.3.5 only applies to inputs collecting personal data where the purpose can be programmatically determined from the WHATWG autocomplete section 4.10.18.7 token list — it does not apply to application-specific fields (e.g., "project name", "task title"); a common mistake is adding `autocomplete="off"` to telephone inputs (to suppress the browser dropdown) which disables assistive technology autofill — this test does not flag `autocomplete="off"` as a violation because some fields legitimately need it (OTP fields), but for personal data fields, `autocomplete="off"` should be treated as a WCAG 1.3.5 failure; add an assertion `expect(actualAutocomplete).not.toBe('off')` inside the loop to catch this anti-pattern.

**Pattern 413** — WCAG 3.1.2 Language of Parts — Verify `lang` Attribute on Non-English Page Sections
```typescript
test('inline foreign language passages have correct lang attribute (WCAG 3.1.2)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/blog/multilingual-post');

  // Find elements explicitly marked with lang attributes
  const langElements = page.locator('[lang]').filter({ hasNot: page.locator('html') });
  const count = await langElements.count();

  // If no lang attributes exist on inline elements, that may itself be a violation
  // when the page contains known foreign phrases — at minimum, verify format
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const el = langElements.nth(i);
    const lang = await el.getAttribute('lang');

    // BCP 47 language tag: 2-3 letter ISO 639 code, optionally with region subtag
    expect(lang).toMatch(/^[a-z]{2,3}(-[A-Z]{2})?(-[a-z]{2,8})*$/);

    // Element must contain actual text content (not just a wrapper)
    const text = await el.textContent();
    expect(text?.trim().length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  }

  // The page lang attribute must exist and be valid
  const htmlLang = await page.locator('html').getAttribute('lang');
  expect(htmlLang).toMatch(/^[a-z]{2,3}(-[A-Z]{2})?(-[a-z]{2,8})*$/);
});
```
Tradeoff: This test validates BCP 47 language tag format and presence but cannot detect missing `lang` attributes on foreign-language passages — it only verifies that elements which already have `lang` attributes have correctly formatted values; detecting missing `lang` attributes requires a human reviewer or a specialised tool like Deque's WorldSpace Attest or manual review with a screen reader set to auto-detect language; additionally, `lang="x-unknown"` is technically a valid private-use subtag in BCP 47 but provides no pronunciation guidance to AT — the regex above correctly rejects it because private-use subtags (`x-`) require at least one subtag separator.

**Pattern 414** — axe-core `wcag22aa` Tag — Run Full WCAG 2.2 AA Scan and Export Structured Violation Report
```typescript
test('page has no WCAG 2.2 AA axe-core violations', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  const { violations } = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa', 'wcag22aa'])
    .analyze();

  // Attach full JSON for CI artifact storage
  await testInfo.attach('axe-wcag22aa-results', {
    body: JSON.stringify(violations, null, 2),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });

  // Structured violation summary for readable failure messages
  const summary = violations.map(v => ({
    id: v.id,
    impact: v.impact,
    wcag: v.tags.filter((t: string) => t.startsWith('wcag')),
    nodeCount: v.nodes.length,
    helpUrl: v.helpUrl,
  }));

  expect(
    violations,
    `WCAG 2.2 AA violations found:\n${JSON.stringify(summary, null, 2)}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: The `wcag22aa` tag in axe-core covers rules introduced for WCAG 2.2 AA criteria specifically (e.g., 2.4.11, 2.5.8, 3.3.7) — however, as of axe-core 4.9.x, not all WCAG 2.2 success criteria have automated rules implemented; 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication) and 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured) have experimental or incomplete rule coverage and may not appear in violation results even when violations exist; use `AxeBuilder.options({ runOnly: { type: 'tag', values: ['wcag22aa'] } })` as an alternative API to restrict the scan to only WCAG 2.2 AA rules, and supplement with manual Patterns 400–403 in this guide for criteria not covered by automated scanning.

### Community Gotchas

**G286** — `role="alertdialog"` requires both `aria-labelledby` and `aria-describedby` — omitting either causes JAWS to read the dialog role without context, leaving the user without information about the dialog's purpose or content when it opens
Why this matters: Developers correctly use `role="alertdialog"` for confirmation dialogs (e.g., "Are you sure you want to delete this item?") because it signals urgency and causes AT to immediately announce the dialog when it opens. However, the ARIA specification requires `alertdialog` to have an accessible name (via `aria-labelledby` pointing to a heading like "Confirm Delete") and an accessible description (via `aria-describedby` pointing to the body text). When `aria-labelledby` is omitted, JAWS 2024 with Chrome announces "alert dialog" with no title, followed by the first focusable element's label — which is typically "OK" or "Cancel". The user hears "alert dialog, OK" with no indication of what they are confirming. NVDA 2024.1 behaves similarly. axe-core rule `dialog-name` flags missing accessible names on dialogs but does not flag missing `aria-describedby` separately — the rule passes if a name exists even without a description, so automated scans may show clean results while the user experience remains severely degraded.
Fix: Always structure alert dialogs as: `<div role="alertdialog" aria-labelledby="dlg-title" aria-describedby="dlg-desc" aria-modal="true">`. Ensure `id="dlg-title"` is on the heading (`<h2 id="dlg-title">Confirm Delete</h2>`) and `id="dlg-desc"` is on the descriptive paragraph (`<p id="dlg-desc">This action cannot be undone...</p>`). Move initial focus to the first actionable button (not the heading) so AT reads the dialog heading, then description, then the button — which gives the user full context before announcing the focus destination. Playwright test: `await expect(page.getByRole('alertdialog')).toHaveAttribute('aria-labelledby', /.+/)`.

**G287** — `inputmode="numeric"` does not set `type="number"` semantics — screen readers still announce the field as a text input, and the numeric virtual keyboard appears on mobile without any AT indication that only digits are expected; combine `inputmode` with `pattern` and an explicit label describing the expected format
Why this matters: `inputmode="numeric"` is commonly used on OTP (one-time password), PIN, and verification code inputs to trigger the numeric keyboard on mobile without the spinner arrows and value sanitisation that `type="number"` introduces. While this is the correct UX pattern (OTPs should use `type="text" inputmode="numeric"` not `type="number"`), the accessible name of such an input typically reads only the label text — e.g., "Verification code". Screen readers do not announce the inputmode restriction. Users with cognitive disabilities or those using AT-driven form filling may not understand that only digits are accepted until they receive a validation error. Combined with `pattern="[0-9]{6}"`, browsers will expose the constraint in the error message, but only after a failed submission. VoiceOver on iOS 16 ignores `inputmode` entirely on some form configurations and shows the full alphanumeric keyboard.
Fix: Include the expected format in the visible label or a linked hint: `<label for="otp">Verification code (6 digits)</label><input id="otp" type="text" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]{6}" aria-describedby="otp-hint"><span id="otp-hint">Enter the 6-digit code from your authenticator app</span>`. The `aria-describedby` hint is announced on focus by all major AT, providing format guidance before the user types. Test that the hint is visible: `await expect(page.locator('#otp-hint')).toBeVisible()` — do not use `sr-only` class for hints that describe format constraints, as sighted users also benefit from the guidance.

**G288** — `aria-expanded` on a `<button>` that controls a sibling `<ul>` dropdown does not create a programmatic relationship between the button and the controlled content — `aria-controls` pointing to the `<ul>` id is required for screen readers to navigate directly from the button to its expanded panel, but browser support for `aria-controls` navigation remains inconsistent across AT
Why this matters: Developers implement disclosure nav menus as `<button aria-expanded="false">Products</button><ul id="products-menu" hidden>`. When the button is focused and activated, `aria-expanded` correctly changes to "true" and AT announces "Products, expanded". However, the user cannot jump from the button to the revealed list using any keyboard shortcut because there is no programmatic ownership relationship. In NVDA with Firefox, `aria-controls` navigation (Insert+Alt+Down) works to jump from button to list. JAWS with Chrome does not support `aria-controls` navigation for disclosure buttons. VoiceOver on macOS ignores `aria-controls` entirely. Because support is inconsistent, some developers omit `aria-controls` and rely on DOM proximity — the list must immediately follow the button in the DOM so AT linear navigation (Tab or arrow keys) naturally reaches the list content next. Putting the list anywhere else in the DOM without `aria-controls` leaves keyboard users stranded.
Fix: Always place the revealed content immediately after its controlling button in the DOM. Add `aria-controls` as a supplementary hint (not primary navigation mechanism): `<button aria-expanded="true" aria-controls="products-menu">Products</button><ul id="products-menu">`. Test navigation by pressing Tab from the button to verify the first item in the opened menu is the next focus stop: `await page.keyboard.press('Tab'); await expect(page.locator('#products-menu li:first-child a')).toBeFocused()`. Do not rely on `aria-controls` navigation as the primary keyboard path; DOM order is the reliable mechanism.

**G289** — CAPTCHA without an audio alternative fails WCAG 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication), but audio CAPTCHAs that require transcribing spoken characters also fail — the only compliant CAPTCHA approaches are object recognition (selecting images), personal content recognition, or removal of CAPTCHA entirely via non-cognitive-test bot detection
Why this matters: Many teams implement audio CAPTCHA as the accessibility alternative to visual CAPTCHA under the assumption that it satisfies both WCAG 1.1.1 (text alternative for non-text content) and accessibility for screen reader users. WCAG 2.2's new SC 3.3.8 (Level AA) changes this analysis: an audio CAPTCHA that plays distorted speech and requires the user to type what they hear is a "transcription" cognitive function test — it requires users to memorise and type a sequence of characters, which is explicitly prohibited under SC 3.3.8. The WCAG Understanding document for 3.3.8 states: "Audio CAPTCHA...unless it is provided as a non-essential alternative" does not pass the criterion. axe-core has no automated rule for SC 3.3.8 as of version 4.9.x, so automated scans will not flag this. The violation is only discoverable through manual audit or code review of the authentication flow.
Fix: Replace transcription-based CAPTCHA with compliant alternatives: (1) image object recognition CAPTCHA where users select images containing a category (e.g., "Click all images with traffic lights") — this tests object perception not memorisation, which the WCAG Understanding document allows; (2) service-side bot detection (e.g., reCAPTCHA v3 invisible scoring, Cloudflare Turnstile) that operates without user interaction; (3) email verification with a link (not a typed code) as the sole authentication step. Test the login flow with a screen reader and document which CAPTCHA variant is present, ensuring paste functionality is available for any code-entry steps.

**G290** — Setting `tabindex` to values greater than `0` (e.g., `tabindex="1"`, `tabindex="5"`) creates a separate, higher-priority tab sequence that is processed before all `tabindex="0"` elements — on large pages this causes keyboard focus to jump unpredictably across the visual layout, breaking WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order
Why this matters: Positive `tabindex` values are frequently added by well-intentioned developers trying to ensure a specific element receives focus early (e.g., a "Search" field with `tabindex="1"` to make it the first Tab stop). In small components this appears to work correctly. However, any element with `tabindex >= 1` on any part of the page — including third-party widgets, injected banners, or analytics scripts — is processed in numeric order before all `tabindex="0"` and natural DOM-order elements. A page with `tabindex="1"` on the search field and `tabindex="2"` on a sidebar widget causes Tab to jump: search → sidebar widget → then loop through the entire remaining page in DOM order. If CSS positions the sidebar on the right, keyboard focus visually jumps right to left, violating WCAG 2.4.3. Lighthouse and axe-core both flag positive `tabindex` values (rule `tabindex`) but the violation is often dismissed as a "warning" rather than actioned.
Fix: Remove all `tabindex` values greater than `0` from the codebase entirely. Use `tabindex="0"` to add non-interactive elements to the natural tab order, and `tabindex="-1"` to allow programmatic focus only. To make an element the first Tab stop on page load, move it to the top of the DOM (before navigation) and use CSS absolute positioning if needed for visual placement — this gives correct DOM order without positive tabindex. Assert the absence of positive tabindex in tests: `const positiveTabindex = await page.locator('[tabindex]').evaluateAll(els => els.filter(el => parseInt(el.getAttribute('tabindex') ?? '0') > 0).map(el => el.outerHTML.slice(0, 100))); expect(positiveTabindex).toHaveLength(0)`.
