**Pattern 8** — axe-core 4.11.2: `aria-errormessage` with multiple IDs and form validation announcement

axe-core 4.11.2 fixed a bug where `aria-errormessage` pointing to multiple space-separated IDs was incorrectly reported as a violation. ARIA 1.2 defines `aria-errormessage` as an ID reference (not a list), but browsers began accepting multiple IDs before the spec was clarified. The 4.11.2 fix ensures axe does not flag multi-ID `aria-errormessage` values as invalid — however, only the **first** ID in the list is reliably resolved by all AT. The correct pattern is a single `aria-errormessage` ID pointing to a container that aggregates all error text.

```typescript
// src/components/FormField/FormField.a11y.test.tsx
import React from 'react';
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { axe, toHaveNoViolations } from 'jest-axe';

expect.extend(toHaveNoViolations);

/**
 * Tests the correct single-ID aria-errormessage pattern.
 * axe-core 4.11.2+: multi-ID aria-errormessage no longer flagged as violation,
 * but single-ID pointing to aggregated error container is still the recommended pattern.
 */
function FieldWithErrors({
  errors,
}: {
  errors: string[];
}) {
  const hasError = errors.length > 0;
  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor="username">Username</label>
      <input
        id="username"
        type="text"
        aria-invalid={hasError ? 'true' : undefined}
        // Single ID pointing to the error container — recommended pattern
        aria-errormessage={hasError ? 'username-errors' : undefined}
        aria-describedby={hasError ? 'username-errors' : undefined}
      />
      {hasError && (
        <div id="username-errors" role="alert" aria-live="assertive">
          {errors.map((err) => (
            <p key={err}>{err}</p>
          ))}
        </div>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

describe('FormField aria-errormessage — axe-core 4.11.2 pattern', () => {
  it('valid state: no axe violations when no errors', async () => {
    const { container } = render(<FieldWithErrors errors={[]} />);
    const results = await axe(container);
    expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
  });

  it('error state: single-ID aria-errormessage passes axe validation', async () => {
    const { container } = render(
      <FieldWithErrors errors={['Username must be at least 3 characters', 'Username cannot contain spaces']} />
    );
    const results = await axe(container);
    // aria-errormessage points to single container with aggregated errors — no violation
    expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
  });

  it('error container is announced by AT — role=alert fires immediately', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const { container, rerender } = render(<FieldWithErrors errors={[]} />);

    // Simulate validation trigger
    rerender(<FieldWithErrors errors={['Field is required']} />);

    // Error message is rendered with role="alert" — fires immediately on mount
    const alert = screen.getByRole('alert');
    expect(alert).toHaveTextContent('Field is required');

    // Verify axe still passes after state change
    const results = await axe(container);
    expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
  });

  it('aria-invalid is set when errors are present', () => {
    render(<FieldWithErrors errors={['Invalid format']} />);
    const input = screen.getByLabelText('Username');
    expect(input).toHaveAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `aria-errormessage` and `aria-describedby` both point to the error container in this pattern. This creates a dual-announcement scenario: `aria-describedby` fires when focus enters the field; `role="alert"` fires when the container is injected. In practice, using both attributes ensures maximum AT coverage — NVDA and JAWS differ in how reliably they announce `aria-errormessage` vs. `aria-describedby` on form validation. The `role="alert"` on the error container guarantees immediate announcement on injection regardless of which AT attribute mechanism is used.

---

**Pattern 9** — `br` and `wbr` elements: axe-core 4.11.3 `aria-allowed-attr` constraint and correct ARIA usage

axe-core 4.11.3 restricted `<br>` and `<wbr>` elements to only accept `aria-hidden` as an allowed ARIA attribute. These elements have no semantic role and exist purely for visual line-breaking purposes. Adding ARIA attributes other than `aria-hidden` to them is a WCAG 4.1.2 failure pattern — the attribute appears in the accessibility tree with no meaningful effect, creating noise for AT.

```typescript
// src/components/Typography/TextBlock.a11y.test.tsx
import React from 'react';
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';
import { axe, toHaveNoViolations } from 'jest-axe';

expect.extend(toHaveNoViolations);

describe('<br> and <wbr> ARIA constraint — axe-core 4.11.3', () => {
  it('<br aria-hidden="true"> is valid — hides from AT', async () => {
    // Use case: address formatting where screen readers should NOT announce line breaks
    const { container } = render(
      <address>
        123 Main Street
        <br aria-hidden="true" />
        Springfield, IL 62701
      </address>
    );
    const results = await axe(container);
    expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
  });

  it('<br> without aria-hidden passes — browser treats it as presentational', async () => {
    // A plain <br> has no ARIA role — it is skipped by AT by default
    const { container } = render(
      <p>
        Line one
        <br />
        Line two
      </p>
    );
    const results = await axe(container);
    expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
  });

  it('detects invalid ARIA attributes on <br> elements (axe-core 4.11.3+)', async () => {
    // This pattern was NOT flagged before 4.11.3 — it is now correctly reported
    const { container } = render(
      // eslint-disable-next-line jsx-a11y/no-interactive-element-to-noninteractive-role
      <div
        dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{
          __html: '<br aria-label="line break" />',
        }}
      />
    );
    const results = await axe(container);
    // aria-label on <br> is now flagged as aria-allowed-attr violation in axe 4.11.3+
    const ariaAttrViolation = results.violations.find((v) => v.id === 'aria-allowed-attr');
    expect(ariaAttrViolation).toBeDefined();
  });

  it('<wbr aria-hidden="true"> is valid — hides soft-hyphen hint from AT', async () => {
    // <wbr> suggests line-break opportunity — aria-hidden suppresses AT announcement
    const { container } = render(
      <code>
        superlong<wbr aria-hidden="true" />variablename
      </code>
    );
    const results = await axe(container);
    expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: The 4.11.3 restriction to `aria-hidden` only on `<br>` and `<wbr>` may break existing codebases that incorrectly use `aria-label` or other ARIA attributes on these elements. Teams upgrading axe-core from 4.11.2 to 4.11.3 should run a full axe scan before and after the upgrade to identify any new `aria-allowed-attr` violations introduced by this stricter enforcement. The correct fix is always to remove the invalid attribute — there is no ARIA attribute other than `aria-hidden` that provides any benefit on a `<br>` or `<wbr>` element.

---

**Pattern 10** — axe DevTools Intelligent Guided Tests (IGTs): extending the 57% automated coverage ceiling in CI

The axe-core automated engine detects approximately 57% of WCAG issues automatically. The remaining ~43% require either manual AT testing or guided semi-automated workflows. Deque's axe DevTools Pro adds Intelligent Guided Tests (IGTs) — AI-driven checks that prompt a tester to answer questions about the UI (e.g., "Is this image decorative?", "Does this form error identify the specific problem?") and use the answer to programmatically classify WCAG compliance. IGTs address success criteria that axe-core cannot determine without human judgment: 1.1.1 (non-text content purpose), 2.4.6 (headings and labels describe topic or purpose), 3.3.2 (visible instructions), and others.

```typescript
// Manual test checklist pattern — TypeScript test scaffold for IGT-equivalent checks
// Use this when axe DevTools Pro IGTs are not available (open-source alternative approach)

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

/**
 * Semi-automated accessibility coverage extender.
 * These tests cover the "gap" between axe-core automated detection and full WCAG coverage.
 * Each test requires human judgment for the final assertion — they are scaffolds, not oracles.
 */
test.describe('Manual-assist A11y patterns (IGT-equivalent coverage)', () => {
  /**
   * WCAG 1.1.1 — Non-text Content
   * axe detects MISSING alt attributes (automated).
   * axe CANNOT detect whether the alt TEXT accurately describes the image (requires human).
   * This test extracts all img alt texts for human review.
   */
  test('extract all image alt texts for human review (WCAG 1.1.1 accuracy gap)', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/products');

    const imageData = await page.evaluate(() => {
      return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('img')).map((img) => ({
        src: img.src.split('/').pop(),
        alt: img.getAttribute('alt'),
        role: img.getAttribute('role'),
        isDecorative: img.getAttribute('alt') === '',
      }));
    });

    // Log for human review — axe can confirm alt presence but not accuracy
    const imagesRequiringReview = imageData.filter(
      (img) => img.alt && img.alt.trim().length > 0 && !img.isDecorative
    );

    console.log(
      `WCAG 1.1.1 human review required for ${imagesRequiringReview.length} descriptive images:`,
      JSON.stringify(imagesRequiringReview, null, 2)
    );

    // Automated assertion: no img missing alt entirely
    const axeResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .withRules(['image-alt'])
      .analyze();
    expect(axeResults.violations).toHaveLength(0);
  });

  /**
   * WCAG 2.4.6 — Headings and Labels Describe Topic or Purpose
   * axe detects heading presence and order (automated).
   * axe CANNOT determine whether heading text is meaningful (requires human).
   */
  test('extract heading structure for human review (WCAG 2.4.6 accuracy gap)', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard');

    const headings = await page.evaluate(() => {
      return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6')).map((h) => ({
        level: h.tagName,
        text: h.textContent?.trim().slice(0, 80),
        ariaLabel: h.getAttribute('aria-label'),
      }));
    });

    console.log('Heading structure (human: verify each heading describes its section):', headings);

    // Automated: heading order is not skipped
    const axeResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .withRules(['heading-order'])
      .analyze();
    expect(axeResults.violations).toHaveLength(0);
  });

  /**
   * WCAG 3.3.2 — Labels or Instructions
   * axe detects missing labels (automated).
   * axe CANNOT determine whether instructions are sufficient for complex inputs (human).
   */
  test('all form inputs have associated labels (WCAG 3.3.2 automated baseline)', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/registration');

    const axeResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .withRules(['label', 'label-title-only', 'label-content-name-mismatch'])
      .analyze();

    expect(axeResults.violations).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: This pattern documents where the boundary between automated and human-judgment testing lies for each WCAG success criterion. The test scaffold extracts data for human review rather than making fully automated assertions — this is intentional. Teams that replace human review with purely automated assertions for criteria like 1.1.1 (alt text accuracy) are creating a false compliance signal. The IGT model (whether via axe DevTools Pro or this manual-assist approach) is the only way to reach genuine >57% WCAG coverage without running a full manual AT audit.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G321** — axe-core's `target-size` rule (WCAG 2.5.8) is **disabled by default** in all axe-core versions — including jest-axe, `@axe-core/playwright`, and the CLI. Running a standard WCAG 2.2 AA axe scan with `withTags(['wcag22aa'])` does NOT include target-size checks unless the rule is explicitly enabled with `.withRules(['target-size'])` or `rules: [{ id: 'target-size', enabled: true }]` [community]
Why this matters: Teams that believe they are testing WCAG 2.2 AA compliance by running axe with `wcag22aa` tags are not testing SC 2.5.8 (Target Size Minimum). The rule's disabled-by-default status means CI gates appear to pass for WCAG 2.2 AA while completely missing target-size violations. This is especially critical for mobile-first products where touch target size is a common failure. The Deque documentation for `target-size` includes a note that the rule is experimental and opt-in, but teams scanning changelog entries or rule-descriptions.md may miss this caveat.
Fix: Add `target-size` to your axe rule configuration explicitly. In `@axe-core/playwright`: `new AxeBuilder({ page }).withRules(['target-size'])`. In jest-axe: `configureAxe({ rules: [{ id: 'target-size', enabled: true }] })`. Add a CI regression test that verifies the rule appears in `results.passes` or `results.violations` (not silently skipped) to confirm opt-in is active.

**G322** — `aria-errormessage` is an ID reference that takes a **single** element ID — passing a space-separated list of IDs (as with `aria-describedby`) is not valid per ARIA 1.2 specification, and AT implementations only resolve the first ID in the list [community]
Why this matters: axe-core 4.11.2 fixed a false-positive that incorrectly flagged space-separated `aria-errormessage` IDs as violations. After the fix, axe no longer reports this pattern as an error — but the AT behavior has not changed. JAWS, NVDA, and VoiceOver all resolve only the first ID in a multi-ID `aria-errormessage` value. Teams who interpret the axe 4.11.2 false-positive fix as "multi-ID aria-errormessage is now valid" will ship code where only the first error message is announced to screen reader users.
Fix: Always use a single ID for `aria-errormessage`, pointing to a container element that aggregates all error text for the field. Use `aria-describedby` (which does accept multiple space-separated IDs) when you need multiple separate descriptions.

**G323** — `<br>` and `<wbr>` elements accept **only** `aria-hidden` as a valid ARIA attribute since axe-core 4.11.3 — adding `aria-label`, `aria-describedby`, or any other ARIA attribute to these elements now triggers an `aria-allowed-attr` violation [community]
Why this matters: Before 4.11.3, teams occasionally added `aria-label` to `<br>` elements to "describe" a line break for screen reader users (e.g., `<br aria-label="new line" />`). This never worked as intended — no AT reads `aria-label` on `<br>` — but axe did not flag it. After upgrading to 4.11.3+, these patterns surface as `aria-allowed-attr` violations. Teams that have suppressions or baselines from pre-4.11.3 scans should clear their baselines and re-scan to catch these newly-detected violations.
Fix: Remove all ARIA attributes from `<br>` and `<wbr>` elements except `aria-hidden="true"` (used to suppress line-break announcements in address or poetry formatting). If a line break needs semantic meaning, restructure the content using a paragraph or list element instead.

**G324** — axe DevTools Intelligent Guided Tests (IGTs) consume AI credits from a Deque account pool — in CI environments where axe DevTools Pro is used, uncontrolled IGT execution on every pull request will deplete AI credits rapidly and may cause CI failures when the credit pool is exhausted [community]
Why this matters: Deque's axe DevTools Pro uses a credit-based model for IGT AI analysis. Each IGT run consumes credits. Teams that integrate axe DevTools Pro into automated CI on every PR commit without credit budgeting will exhaust their monthly allocation within days on active repositories. The IGT failure mode is a CI error message about insufficient credits, not a meaningful accessibility violation report — testers may misinterpret this as a passing scan.
Fix: Configure IGT runs to execute only on scheduled nightly scans or manually-triggered release gates, not on every push. Use the standard axe-core automated scan (no credits required) for PR gates. Reserve IGTs for pre-release audits and regression baselines. Monitor credit consumption via the Deque dashboard.

**G325** — axe-core 4.11.0's `aria-prohibited-attr` rule catches ARIA attributes that are explicitly forbidden for a given role (e.g., `aria-checked` on a `role="button"`) — this is distinct from `aria-allowed-attr` which catches attributes that are simply not in the allowed list for a role [community]
Why this matters: ARIA 1.2 distinguishes between attributes that are "allowed" for a role (optional, may be present) and attributes that are "prohibited" for a role (must not be present even if technically valid global ARIA). The `aria-prohibited-attr` rule (added in axe-core 4.11.0) surfaces cases where prohibited attributes are present — these often arise when refactoring a component from one role to another (e.g., changing `role="checkbox"` to `role="button"` without removing `aria-checked`). Before 4.11.0, this pattern was not flagged by axe.
Fix: After any ARIA role change on a component, run an axe scan and check for both `aria-allowed-attr` and `aria-prohibited-attr` violations. When migrating a component from a state-bearing role (checkbox, radio, switch) to a non-state role (button, link), systematically audit all ARIA attributes and remove any that are prohibited for the new role.
